papers.title: Integrated Single‐Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Convergence on a Senescence‐Associated B Cell–MIF Signaling Axis in Joint Aging and Osteoarthritis Progression
papers.authors: Weida Li; Yi Wang; Yongqing You; Yue Cui; Jiayun Liu; Xingbiao Ma; QiuYu Zhu; Qiang Wu; Zanjing Zhai; Zuyan Lu; Kerong Dai; Ye Sun
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Osteoarthritis (OA) involves age‐associated structural and immune changes, yet whether senescence‐associated B‐cell states contribute to cartilage degeneration remains unclear. Integrated single‐cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of healthy, aged, and OA mouse joints identify reduced B‐cell abundance but enrichment of a low‐proliferative, inflammatory state with heightened macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) signaling. Cell–cell communication and spatial ligand–receptor analyses identify enhanced predicted MIF–CD74/CD44 interactions in B‐cell‐associated regions adjacent to cartilage. Constitutive MIF deficiency attenuates senescence‐associated B‐cell changes, MMP13 induction, and cartilage damage in vivo. Joint‐derived B cells from aged and OA mice induce chondrocyte senescence, reduce COL2A1 and HMGB1, and increase FN1 and MMP13 through MIF‐dependent paracrine signaling. These effects are suppressed by MIF neutralization and restored by recombinant MIF in MIF‐deficient co‐cultures. A composite hydrogel carrying quercetin and MIF‐siRNA‐loaded PLGA microspheres for local co‐delivery. The microspheres show gradual siRNA release over 96 h in vitro. In DMM‐induced OA, the formulation reduces MIF, P16, and MMP13 signals, restores HMGB1, and preserves cartilage. These findings support a senescence‐associated B cell–MIF signaling axis associated with joint aging and chondrocyte dysfunction and provide proof of concept for a local biomaterial‐based strategy that attenuates OA‐associated changes.

papers.title: A Damage‐Gated Small‐Molecule Chimera Selectively Enhances Mitophagy by Coupling Dysfunctional Mitochondria to Autophagy
papers.authors: Ratislav M. Ozhiganov; Ekaterina А. Guseva; Alexander Yu. Rudenko; Konstantin G. Lyamzaev; Sofya Y. Sokolskaya; Julia A. Golubeva; Maria V. Belopolskaya; Nadezda V. Andrianova; Olga V. Fadeeva; Elena О. Morgun; Elena A. Tukhovskaya; Marina S. Kazakova; Vladimir M. Pavlov; Daria K. Yagoda; Elena I. Marusich; Rose‐Lys Zaranaina; Valeriya B. Vays; Irina M. Vangeli; Egor Y. Plotnikov; Maxim L. Lovat; Lora E. Bakeeva; Arkady N. Murashev; Vladimir I. Polshakov; Olga A. Dontsova; Peter V. Sergiev
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Mitophagy is a central mitochondrial quality‐control pathway, and its pharmacological activation is considered to be geroprotective. However, its small‐molecule activators act indirectly by perturbing metabolism or mitochondrial function, limiting selectivity and increasing toxicity. Here, we describe a chemical biology strategy for activating damage‐responsive mitophagy using bifunctional small molecules that couple mitochondrial recognition to the recruitment of the autophagic machinery. We designed and synthesized a focused library of chimeric molecules and identified MG‐1 as a lead compound. It had minimal effects on basal autophagy but markedly enhanced autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance under conditions of mitochondrial stress. Biochemical analyses, together with fluorescence and electron microscopy, showed that MG‐1 promotes lysosomal degradation of damaged mitochondria without acting as a direct mitochondrial uncoupler. MG‐1 was well tolerated across experimental systems and improved locomotor performance in a zebrafish model of MPTP‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings establish damage‐gated small‐molecule chimeras as a promising approach for selective control of mitochondrial quality.

papers.title: HFPO‑TA induces developmental hepatotoxicity in hESC‑derived hepatocyte‑like cells by disrupting lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial function.
papers.authors: Sujie Sun; Hao Chen; Yi Hu; Zhenying Lin; Haoran Ye; Qianqian Zhang; Jiuru Zhao; Xiaorui Liu; Zhiwei Liu
papers.abstract: Hexafluoropropylene oxide trimer acid (HFPO-TA), an alternative to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), can cross the placental barrier, raising concerns regarding fetal hepatic development; however, the mechanisms underlying its developmental hepatotoxicity remain poorly elucidated. Here, human embryonic stem cell-derived hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs) were exposed to HFPO-TA at 3, 15, or 75μM for 28 days during hepatocytic differentiation. HFPO-TA accumulated intracellularly in a dose- and time-dependent manner and impaired hepatic function, evidenced by reduced albumin secretion and CYP activity and increased alanine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels. Integrated proteomic and metabolomic profiling revealed extensive disruption of lipid metabolism, including increased triglycerides, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein levels, and decreased high-density lipoprotein levels. HFPO-TA activated PPAR signaling and altered genes and proteins associated with lipid synthesis and oxidation, with significant perturbations even at the environmentally relevant concentration of 3 μM. Oil Red O staining and altered PLIN1 and PLIN2 expression confirmed lipid droplet accumulation. HFPO-TA also disrupted mitochondrial function, altered respiratory chain activity, reduced ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential, and up-regulated fission-fusion-related genes. Collectively, these findings indicate that HFPO-TA impairs hepatocyte differentiation through PPAR-mediated lipid remodeling and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting safety concerns for this PFOA alternative. Furthermore, HLCs are a valuable in vitro model for assessing the developmental toxicity of PFOA alternatives.

papers.title: Temporal Changes in Hepatic Fatty Acid Metabolism, Desaturase Expression, and Lipid Peroxidation During Long-Term Sucrose Feeding in Male and Female Rats
papers.authors: Sunčica Heštera; Tomislav Mašek; Petra Roginek; Maja Maurić Maljković; Vedran Micek; Kristina Starčević
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic sucrose consumption may contribute to progressive metabolic dysfunction, but the combined influence of long-term exposure, aging, sex, and dietary fiber on hepatic lipid metabolism remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated how time and sex influence hepatic lipid metabolism during chronic sucrose supplementation and characterized responses under different dietary backgrounds. Methods: A total of 120 Wistar Han rats (60 males and 60 females) were allocated to four dietary treatments: control diet (CON), control diet with increased fiber content (CON-fiber), 30% sucrose in drinking water (HS), or 30% sucrose in drinking water with high fiber content (HS-fiber). Five animals of each sex per treatment were euthanized after 1, 12, or 24 months. Glucose homeostasis, hepatic fatty-acid composition, serum malondialdehyde (MDA), and hepatic expression of SCD1, Fads1, Fads2, NRF2, TNFα, and TGFβ were evaluated. Results: Treatment effects became prominent after 12 and 24 months. Chronic sucrose intake increased body mass in HS rats, impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, shifted the hepatic fatty-acid profile toward monounsaturated fatty acids, and reduced several n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids. Increased SCD1 expression accompanied increased relative proportions of palmitoleic and oleic acids, whereas Fads1 and Fads2 showed treatment-associated differences within individual sampling points. Sucrose-exposed groups also developed increased lipid peroxidation and a pro-inflammatory transcriptional response. Conclusions: Metabolic, oxidative, and inflammatory alterations were observed in sucrose-fed groups, with treatment-associated differences depending on sex and sampling time point. These findings emphasize the importance of exposure duration and biological sex in shaping metabolic responses during aging.

papers.title: Lipids at the meningeal-tumor interface: aging, anatomical niches, and meningioma biology
papers.authors: Michele Cerasuolo; Nicholas Giulio Raccagni; Simone Laguardia; Gary Antonio Barahona Rodriguez
papers.abstract: Meningiomas exhibit substantial molecular, anatomical, and microenvironmental heterogeneity, yet the spatial organization of their lipid biology remains poorly understood. Emerging lipidomic studies demonstrate extensive remodeling of membrane, signaling, and mitochondrial lipid classes, with profiles varying according to molecular genotype, histopathological grade, and potentially patient characteristics. In parallel, developmental, single-cell, and spatial studies have revealed the meninges and meningiomas as regionally organized systems comprising distinct stromal, vascular, immune, and neoplastic populations. Here, we integrate these lines of evidence and propose the aging meningeal lipid niche as an anatomically grounded framework for understanding lipid biology across the meningioma–meningeal interface. We examine the dural attachment and tumor–bone interface, perivascular niche, immune-enriched regions, tumor core, and tumor–brain boundary as candidate metabolic compartments in which cellular composition, vascular access, extracellular architecture, and inflammatory signaling may shape local lipid states. We further consider how aging may modify these environments through remodeling of the meningeal extracellular matrix, lymphatic function, immune composition, and lipid homeostasis, while distinguishing direct evidence in meningioma from mechanistic inference. A central limitation of current studies is their reliance on bulk tissue, which precludes confident attribution of lipid signals to specific anatomical and cellular sources. We therefore outline a spatially resolved strategy integrating anatomically registered sampling with mass spectrometry imaging, histopathology, molecular classification, and single-cell or spatial transcriptomic approaches. This framework provides testable hypotheses to determine whether meningioma lipid states reflect tumor-intrinsic programs, anatomically defined microenvironments, aging-associated remodeling, or interactions among these determinants, and how these states relate to invasion, recurrence, edema, and treatment resistance.

papers.title: Red Light Therapy and Mitochondrial Rejuvenation in Age-Related Disorders.
papers.authors: Maria Iglewska; Kinga Agata Flis; Maja Kołakowska; Witold Wit Hryniewicz; Agnieszka Pluto-Prądzyńska
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired ATP production, and a decline in tissue regenerative capacity, leading to the development of age-related diseases. This review summarizes current evidence regarding the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) on mitochondrial function and age-related disorders. PBM using red and near-infrared light may enhance proper mitochondrial function by acting on cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) and other signaling pathways, including the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel, leading to increased ATP production, modulation of ROS signaling, and improved cellular homeostasis. We review in vitro, animal, and clinical studies investigating PBM in metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, cardiovascular, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and skeletal muscle disorders associated with aging, as well as its application in the management of cancer therapy-related oral mucositis. Current studies demonstrate beneficial effects on glucose metabolism, cardiovascular function, neuronal function, lipid metabolism, liver function, muscle regeneration, and visual function in AMD, as well as the safety and efficacy of PBM in the management of cancer therapy-induced oral mucositis. The therapeutic effects of PBM appear to be dose-dependent and influenced by treatment parameters including wavelength, fluence, irradiance, and exposure protocol. Although photobiomodulation still lacks standardized treatment protocols and differences exist in the wavelengths used, dosage, and frequency among studies, it represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of age-related diseases.

papers.title: The crosstalk between ferroptosis and cellular senescence in gestational diabetes mellitus: from iron dyshomeostasis to trophoblast dysfunction
papers.authors: Min Li; Wendi Zhao; Lei Jiang; Yijing Chu
papers.abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) comprises heterogeneous placental phenotypes that include fetal overgrowth, large-for-gestational-age birth, and fetal growth restriction (FGR). We propose a testable endotype model in which maternal hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end products, diabetic dyslipidemia, altered polyunsaturated fatty-acid delivery, gestational iron exposure, and the physiologic fall in hepcidin converge on a redox-stressed trophoblast microenvironment. In proliferative cytotrophoblasts and extravillous trophoblasts, the relative reserve of GPX4 and FSP1/CoQ10, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-phospholipid loading, proliferative status, and insult intensity and duration are predicted to determine whether cells undergo ferroptosis, enter senescence, or occupy an intermediate state. We further propose an asymmetric crosstalk model: senescent trophoblasts are relatively ferroptosis-resistant, retain iron, and act in trans through SASP factors, reactive oxygen species, and oxidized lipids on ferroptosis-susceptible neighboring cells. The model predicts a gestational-age-dependent window in which physiologic senescence accumulates and its paracrine effects become injurious. Ferrostatin-1 or liproxstatin-1 should rescue lipid-peroxidation-driven death in susceptible cells without reversing senescence in iron-retaining cells. The model is GDM-specific in its initiating inputs and gestational context, but the reciprocal links remain hypotheses rather than established facts. It predicts that an injury-dominant placental endotype will show spatially adjacent iron-retaining senescence-like cells and lipid-peroxidation-driven cell death, impaired nutrient transport, and FGR, whereas compensatory transport and villous expansion may produce large-for-gestational-age phenotypes in other GDM placentas. We outline experiments that could support or falsify this model and define pregnancy-specific safety constraints for therapeutic testing.

papers.title: Beyond Chronological Age: Circadian Disruption, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, and the Biology of Female Reproductive Aging
papers.authors: Warda Abubakar; Laiba Rehmat
papers.venue: Journal of Women's Health, Reproductive Medicine and Physiology
papers.abstract: Female reproductive aging involves progressive follicular depletion, declining oocyte competence, and changes in reproductive endocrine function. This narrative review examines the potential interactions between circadian regulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress in ovarian aging. Evidence on sleep timing, shift work, ovarian clock genes, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and redox homeostasis is considered. Although these processes share pathways involved in cellular metabolism and stress regulation, direct evidence that circadian disruption accelerates ovarian reserve depletion or shortens reproductive lifespan in humans remains limited. The proposed circadian–mitochondrial relationship should therefore be considered a testable hypothesis rather than an established causal pathway. Longitudinal human studies integrating objective circadian measures, ovarian reserve markers, mitochondrial assessments, and reproductive outcomes are needed to clarify these interactions and their clinical significance.

papers.title: Curcumin mitigates palmitic acid-induced senescence in MIN6 β cells through NOX4/ROS regulation.
papers.authors: Zhanhong Guo; Huan Zhang; Ming Shi; Yinghong Kong
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pancreatic β cell senescence is a key driver of type 2 diabetes (T2D) progression, and oxidative stress plays a critical role in this process. This study explored the therapeutic potential of curcumin against palmitic acid (PA)-induced senescence in MIN6 cells. We also explored whether this protection was achieved via modulation of the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase 4 (NOX4)/reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathway. METHODS: We used PA to establish a lipotoxicity model in MIN6 cells. We assessed cell viability by Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay and insulin secretion with glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) assay. We used flow cytometry to measure calcium concentration, β-galactosidase activity, cell cycle distribution, ROS production and mitochondrial membrane potential. Western blot was used to analyze the expression of NOX4 and senescence markers p16 and p21. We also performed molecular docking to predict the binding mode between curcumin and NOX4. We knocked down NOX4 to confirm its role in curcumin's protective effects. RESULTS: PA significantly reduced MIN6 cell viability, insulin secretion and intracellular calcium concentration. PA induced cellular senescence, as evidenced by increased β-galactosidase activity, upregulated p16 and p21 expression and cell cycle arrest in the G0/G1 phase. PA activated the NOX4/ROS pathway, leading to ROS overproduction and a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential. Curcumin treatment partially reversed these effects. Molecular docking showed curcumin binds strongly to NOX4 (binding energy: -8.4 kcal/mol). NOX4 knockdown enhanced curcumin's effects on oxidative stress and cell senescence. CONCLUSION: Curcumin mitigates PA-induced senescence in MIN6 cells and restores insulin secretion by inhibiting the overactivation of the NOX4/ROS pathway and reducing oxidative stress.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture regulates lipid metabolism through PPARγ-associated LXRα signaling: from nuclear receptor signaling to cardiovascular protection
papers.authors: Shuyan Zhang; Jihao Yang; Xinhao Yan; Haichun Zhou
papers.abstract: Hyperlipidemia is an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and a substantial proportion of patients remain inadequately controlled on statin therapy because single-target interventions cannot fully reverse the systemic inflammation and tissue injury driven by dysregulated lipid metabolism. Electroacupuncture (EA), a modern refinement of traditional acupuncture,has been reported to lower serum total cholesterol, triglycerides, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in clinical trials, yet the molecular basis of these effects has not been systematically synthesized. Here, we review the evidence that EA regulates lipid homeostasis through the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPAR γ )/liver X receptor α (LXR α ) axis. We first outline the structure and function of these nuclear receptors and their transcriptional crosstalk, and then examine how EA modulates their expression, activity, and co-regulators. We next trace the upstream signal transduction from somatic afferent activation through the neuro–endocrine–immune network, and the downstream effector programs, including cholesterol efflux, fatty-acid oxidation, macrophage M2 polarization, and organ-specific cardiovascular protection. Pharmacological antagonism, PPAR γ knockdown, and MerTK deficiency provide causal evidence that the PPAR γ -associated efferocytic program contributes to the lipid-lowering and efferocytic effects of EA, whereas the involvement of LXR α is supported primarily by its coordinated expression with PPAR γ and downstream cholesterol-efflux signaling. We conclude by discussing the heterogeneity of EA parameters, the animal-to-human translational gap, and the limitations of causal inference in the current literature, and outline future directions, including optogenetic dissection of acupuncture neural circuits and PPAR γ /LXR α -guided standardization of EA protocols.

papers.title: Inhibiting apolipoprotein C3 alleviates ferroptosis and cell damage induced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
papers.authors: Yaoyang Liu; Xuejing Yang; Tianchun Ni; Jialu Zong; Chen Qian; Xudong Wang; Juan Yu
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To explore the induction effect of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) infection on ferroptosis and inflammatory response in human hepatoma cells (Hep3B) and the regulatory effect of apolipoprotein C3(APOC3) on ferroptosis sensitivity. METHODS: Hep3B hepatocytes (MOI=5, 10, 15) were infected with the wild standard strain of PA (PAO1) for 4 h, 8 h, and 12 h respectively, and the survival rate of cells under different infection concentrations and times was detected by CCK-8. The morphological changes of cells were observed under an inverted microscope to determine the infection conditions. After adding ferroptosis inhibitors or siRNA respectively to inhibit the expression of APOC3, lipid droplets were labeled using oil red O staining, and the formation of lipid droplets was observed under an inverted microscope. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) were detected using a fluorescent probe (DCFH-DA), and lipid peroxidation levels were detected using a microplate reader. The expression levels of Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor α (PPARα), APOC3 and related inflammatory factors were detected by RT-qPCR. The protein expression levels of APOC3 and the ferroptosis-related proteins SLC7A11 and ACSL4 were evaluated by Western blotting. The morphological changes of mitochondria in cells were observed by transmission electron microscopy. The content of Fe2+ in cells was detected using a divalent iron ion probe. RESULTS: With the increase of infection concentration and the extension of time, the survival rate of Hep3B cells significantly decreased after PAO1 infection, and the cell morphology gradually changed from spindle-shaped to round and accompanied by fragmentation. The number of red lipid droplets within the cells increased with the increase of the bacterial load. The fluorescence intensity of ROS was enhanced. The expression of PPARα mRNA was down-regulated and the expression of APOC3 mRNA was up-regulated. The volume of mitochondria decreased, the membrane density increased, and the cristae were reduced or even disappeared. Western blotting further confirmed the changes in APOC3 protein expression and ferroptosis-related proteins, including SLC7A11 and ACSL4, following PAO1 infection and APOC3 knockdown. The intracellular lipid peroxidation level was significantly increased. Compared with the control group, the levels of IL-6 and TNF-α significantly increased after PA infection. After inhibiting the expression of APOC3, the expression level of ROS decreased, lipid peroxidation reduced, the number of lipid droplets decreased, the content of Fe2+ decreased, mitochondrial damage decreased, and the expression of ferroptosis-related factors decreased. CONCLUSION: After the action of PA, cell activity significantly decreased, intracellular ROS generation increased, and intracellular lipid peroxidation was enhanced, leading to cell damage and death. Meanwhile, APOC3, as a key downstream target of PPARα, PA promotes the generation of APOC3 by inhibiting the expression of PPARα, and APOC3 reduces the hydrolysis of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL), thereby promoting lipid droplet formation. It causes the accumulation of lipids within cells. However, the continuous inhibitionof APOC3 can reverse this effect. That is, after PA infects cells, it can promote the increase of APOC3 expression, leading to lipid metabolism disorders, and APOC3 plays a promoting role in the process of PA promoting ferroptosis in cells.

papers.title: Omega-3 fatty acids in aromatase inhibitor-associated dyslipidemia: mechanisms, clinical evidence, and future perspectives
papers.authors: Ruiqi Chen; Minghao Xiong; Shengchao Huang
papers.abstract: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs), including anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane, are widely used as adjuvant endocrine therapy for postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. However, prolonged estrogen deprivation induced by AI therapy may adversely affect lipid homeostasis and has been associated with alterations in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol (TC), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), potentially contributing to long-term cardiovascular risk. The mechanisms underlying these abnormalities appear to involve estrogen-dependent regulation of hepatic lipoprotein metabolism, together with endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), have established effects on lipid metabolism and cardiovascular health. Their metabolic actions include activation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-α (PPAR-α), suppression of sterol regulatory element-binding protein-1c (SREBP-1c), modulation of hepatic very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) production, enhancement of fatty acid oxidation, and regulation of lipoprotein clearance. However, the effects of EPA and DHA on LDL-C, TC, and HDL-C are less consistent than their triglyceride-lowering effects and may differ according to formulation and dose. In this review, we critically examine the biological mechanisms underlying AI-associated dyslipidemia, compare the lipid effects of individual AIs with tamoxifen, and evaluate the potential mechanisms through which EPA and DHA may modulate cholesterol and lipoprotein metabolism. We further summarize clinical evidence from general dyslipidemia and breast cancer populations and assess its applicability to patients receiving AI therapy. Current evidence supports a strong biological rationale for omega-3 fatty acid supplementation but remains insufficient to establish its efficacy specifically for AI-associated dyslipidemia. Future randomized controlled trials should directly evaluate lipid and cardiovascular outcomes, compare EPA- and DHA-containing formulations, account for differences among individual AIs, and identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from omega-3-based interventions.

papers.title: Integrated chemical profiling and lipidomics reveal that Mailuoning oral liquid alleviates diet-induced MASLD via PPARα-mediated lipid homeostasis and COX-2 inhibition, with identification of potential active constituents
papers.authors: Sijia Wu; Wangya Jia; Xun Zhou; Linyan Zhu; Keke Wang; Jian Li; Lili Ji; Wei Liu; Hong Xu
papers.abstract: Background Mailuoning oral liquid (MLN), a standardized five-herb formula, is used for ischemic vascular diseases and shows potential in ameliorating dyslipidemia. Our previous study showed MLN alleviates metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) via peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) activation, but its comprehensive chemical profile, systemic exposure, and bioactive constituents mediating both PPARα activation and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibition remain unclear. Methods High-fat, high-fructose diet-fed rats received MLN (5.4 or 10.8 mL/kg/day) for 8 weeks. Ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap HRMS) profiled MLN chemicals and identified serum/liver prototypes. Biochemical profiles, glucose tolerance, histopathology, untargeted lipidomics, and targeted polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) analysis were performed. PPARα and COX-2 signaling were examined by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. Key constituents were screened for PPARα activation via dual luciferase reporter assay and molecular docking; COX-2 inhibition was validated by enzyme assays and molecular dynamics. Results A total of 143 compounds were characterized; 48 and 92 prototypes were enriched in serum and liver, respectively. MLN ameliorated dyslipidemia, glucose intolerance, steatosis, and inflammation. Lipidomics revealed bidirectional modulation of hepatic lipids, reversing triglyceride (TAG) accumulation and restoring phosphatidylcholine (PC) and lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) levels. Targeted analysis showed increased eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and normalized COX-2-derived prostaglandins (PGD 2 , PGE 2 ). MLN activated hepatic PPARα and downregulated COX-2. Seven serum-enriched compounds (chlorogenic acid, macranthoidin B, luteoloside, harpagide, angoroside C, oleanolic acid, betaine) were validated as direct PPARα agonists. Secologanoside and chikusetsusaponin IVa were identified as novel COX-2 inhibitors (half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) = 14.61 and 120.9 nM). Discussion MLN alleviates MASLD via dual PPARα activation and COX-2 inhibition, providing a mechanistic foundation for repurposing this herbal formula in early-stage MASLD.

papers.title: Plasma Lipidomic Features of Adolescent Major Depressive Disorder and Lipid Changes After Fluoxetine Treatment
papers.authors: Chenxi Liu; Yao Li; Hanchen Hou; Jiamei Guo; Bingjie Qin; Xiaoxia Xu; Yuqian He; Tingting Lei; Fei Chen; Lige Zhang; Quanbing Liu; Li Gao; Jiaqi Shi; Haoran Xing; Teng Teng; Tian Qiu; Xinyu Zhou
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a major public health concern, yet objective biological markers and treatment‐related metabolic changes remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize plasma lipidomic alterations in adolescent MDD and explore lipid changes associated with fluoxetine treatment. Methods This study enrolled 75 adolescents with MDD and 75 matched healthy controls (HCs). Among the adolescents with MDD, 44 had paired baseline and week‐8 plasma samples available and were included in the longitudinal analysis. Plasma lipidomic profiles were analyzed using ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC–MS/MS). Results A total of 865 lipid species were detected. Compared with HCs, adolescents with MDD showed distinct plasma lipidomic profiles, with 82 differentially abundant lipid species identified, primarily involving triglycerides, lysophospholipids, free fatty acids, membrane phospholipids, and sphingolipids. Among the machine‐learning models, logistic regression showed the highest discriminative performance, with a pooled out‐of‐fold AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79–0.91). Longitudinal analysis identified 21 lipid species meeting the differential criteria following fluoxetine treatment, mainly involving triglycerides and bile acid‐related metabolites. Integrative pathway and target analyses suggested that fluoxetine‐associated lipid changes may involve neurotransmitter signaling, inflammatory lipid metabolism, PI3K–Akt signaling, and nuclear receptor‐related pathways. Conclusion This study characterizes alterations in plasma lipid metabolism in adolescent MDD and the lipidomic changes following fluoxetine treatment, providing new lipidomic evidence for candidate lipid signatures and potential treatment‐associated biological pathways. papers.title: A stress-adapted fiber state promotes clonal expansion of deleted mitochondrial DNA.
papers.authors: Diego Perez-Rodriguez; Ilaria Dalla Rosa; Anastasia Magoulopoulou; Sara Ricciardi; Samantha Davidson; Rebecca Lasalandra; Renata Kabiljo; Aine Moylett; Tamara Hill; Tengfei Wan; Aleck W E Jones; Chloe F Moss; Charlotte Zierz; Melissa L Salazar; Radha Desai; Shar-Yin N Huang; Yves Pommier; Monika Hofer; Robert D S Pitceathly; Martin A M Reijns; Joanna Poulton; Christos Proukakis; J Paul Simons; Mats Nilsson; Robert W Taylor; Ian J Holt; Antonella Spinazzola
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion and multiple deletions frequently coexist in mitochondrial disease, neurodegeneration, and aging, yet how the two relate and why deletions accumulate focally remain unresolved. Here, longitudinal bulk and in situ analyses of Mpv17-/- murine muscle reveal that a compensatory rise in mitochondrial transcripts per mtDNA initially offsets severe, uniform mtDNA depletion, preserving the respiratory chain. However, this response carries a delayed cost: by six months transcripts decline, mtDNA deletions emerge, and respiratory-deficient fibers appear. Paradoxically, fibers harboring deletions accumulate supra-physiological amounts of mtDNA, despite prior depletion. This expansion is invariably accompanied by elevated Hsp60, and the same holds in human mitochondrial myopathy. We propose that depletion reprograms mitochondrial DNA and RNA metabolism, inadvertently promoting deletion formation and creating an Hsp60-high fiber state permissive for clonal expansion. Therefore, depletion and multiple deletions can be sequential phases of a common degenerative process, relevant also to aging and neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Mitochondrial acquisition after the Asgard revolution: Reconstructing eukaryogenesis with insights for mitochondrial transplantation.
papers.authors: Yuan-Yuan Li; Kevin B Frazier; Franklin R Tay
papers.abstract: Mitochondria arose from an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont that became integrated within an archaeal host during eukaryogenesis. The discovery of Asgard archaea has clarified host ancestry and supports reconstructions in which aspects of cytoskeletal and membrane complexity preceded mitochondrial acquisition. Organellogenesis involved genome reduction, gene transfer, protein import, metabolic coupling, and vertical inheritance. These evolutionary principles complement current mitochondrial transplantation recommendations by generating testable predictions about recipient dependence and the duration of rescue. Transplanted mitochondria are mature organelles introduced into cells already equipped to maintain mitochondria; the requirement for transient or durable function must nevertheless be tested for each indication. Aging can modify organelle delivery, recipient quality control, and tissue responses, with particular implications for the neurovascular unit and neuronal function. Extracellular vesicle delivery requires verification of mitochondrial cargo, potency, and compatibility. Measurable criteria distinguish delivery, uptake, cytosolic access, network interaction, persistence, and functional benefit, while separating evidence from aging, acute ischemia, and inherited disease models.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction as a Convergent Mechanism of α-Synuclein Toxicity: A Systematic Review of In Vitro Fibrillar Models.
papers.authors: Hanadi Al Tbeishat; Douglas G Ward; Ilse S Pienaar; Richard J Elsworthy
papers.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy bodies, and Multiple System Atrophy, are characterised by intracellular accumulation of misfolded α-synuclein (αSyn). Although αSyn aggregation is central to disease pathogenesis, the mechanisms linking αSyn to progressive neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood. Mitochondrial dysfunction is recognised as a key pathological process, particularly in experimental models using exogenously applied αSyn species, including preformed fibrils (PFFs). This systematic review synthesises evidence from mammalian in vitro studies that examined the effects of disease-associated αSyn conformations, including monomers, oligomers and PFFs, on mitochondrial structure and function. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycInfo were searched to identify eligible peer-reviewed studies published up to March 2026, yielding 33 included studies. Models encompassed neuronal, astrocytic, microglial, endothelial, fibroblast, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived systems, enabling comparison across cell types, αSyn conformations, and genetic backgrounds. Across included studies, oligomeric and fibrillar αSyn consistently induced mitochondrial depolarisation, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, reduced ATP production, complex-I dysfunction and increased reactive oxygen species generation. Additional mitochondrial pathological changes included fragmentation, cristae disruption, impaired TOM20-mediated protein import, calcium dysregulation, defective mitophagy and increased heteroplasmy i.e. accumulation of damaged mitochondria. These alterations frequently preceded cell death and were amplified in dopaminergic and genetically vulnerable models, including αSyn A53T, SNCA triplication, and PARK2-associated transgenic systems. Our review highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as a mechanism underlying αSyn toxicity, whilst suggesting methodological heterogeneity can limit cross-study translation. Priorities for future research using 'in vitro' models of PFF synucleinopathies include standardised fibril preparation protocols, improved mitochondrial phenotyping, and use of human multicellular and organoid models.

papers.title: Involvement of PINK1-related Mitophagy and Necroptosis in TDI-Induced Experimental Asthma.
papers.authors: Xiu He; Shuai Fu; Dengxiang Yao; Lijuan Zuo; Xiaoli Yuan; Yiyang Du; Zhiyao Qian; Jiaqi Ban; Qian He; Mingdan You
papers.abstract: Toluene diisocyanate (TDI) is a prevalent cause of occupational asthma. Although mitophagy contributes to various pulmonary diseases, its role and downstream signaling in TDI-induced asthma remain unclear. In this study, we first utilized BALB/c mice to investigate the effects of TDI exposure on pulmonary injury, mitophagy, and associated regulatory mechanisms. Based on these findings, we constructed an adverse outcome pathway (AOP) network for TDI-induced asthma. Mechanistic connections predicted by the AOP were validated in vitro using PINK1-knockdown bronchial epithelial cells, assessing PINK1-related mitophagy, mitochondrial function, cytosolic mtDNA release, attenuated the increased expression of cGAS/STING pathway-related proteins, and necroptosis. Finally, we predicted potential natural product therapeutics through bioactivity screening and toxicity profiling, targeting key genes implicated in TDI-induced asthma. Integration of in vivo, in vitro, and AOP network analyses indicated that TDI exposure induced airway hyperresponsiveness and pulmonary histopathological changes, along with elevated Th2 cytokine production. This exposure selectively upregulated PINK1 and Parkin expression, without altering levels of BNIP3, NIX, or FUNDC1. PINK1 knockdown mitigated TDI-induced mitophagy-related alterations, restored mitochondrial function, reduced cytosolic mtDNA release, attenuated the increased expression of cGAS/STING pathway-related proteins, and reduced necroptosis. In silico screening predicted β-lapachone, genistein, and apigenin as promising candidate therapeutics for TDI-induced asthma. Overall, PINK1-related mitophagy may contribute to TDI-induced occupational asthma, and natural compounds identified via in silico screening are potential candidates that require further in vitro and in vivo validation of their safety and efficacy.

papers.title: Transcriptomic signatures of lipids in blood provide hypotheses of functional mechanisms linked to lipid metabolism and immune-cell regulation.
papers.authors: Jessica I Lundin; Mariaelisa Graff; Jeff Haessler; Xinruo Zhang; Yanwei Cai; Harriett Fuller; Nancy Heard-Costa; Tianxiao Huan; Roby Joehanes; Joshua M Landman; Gina Marie Peloso; Yuxuan Wang; Zhe Wang; Jennifer E Below; Daniel Levy; Kari E North; Alex P Reiner; Ryan Zukowski; Ulrike Peters; Charles Kooperberg
papers.abstract: Blood lipids are well-established risk factors for cardiovascular and other chronic diseases, yet the underlying functional mechanisms remain unclear. We conducted a large-scale, genome-wide transcriptome analysis of serum lipid levels using whole blood RNA-sequencing data from 6898 individuals of diverse races and ethnicities (17% Black or African American, 15% Hispanic Latino/a, 68% White). We utilized mixed-effects linear regression and meta-analyzed four discovery datasets (n = 4398 participants), identifying significant associations for 27 genes with low-density lipoproteins (LDL), 974 with high-density lipoproteins (HDL), 1229 with triglycerides (TRIG), and 276 with total cholesterol (TCHO). Two replication datasets (n = 2500 participants) confirmed 3, 55, 380, and 31 genes, respectively. Enrichment analysis revealed lipid metabolic processes for LDL, HDL, and TCHO associated genes, including LDLR, NPC2, and SQLE for LDL and TCHO, while TRIG associated genes highlighted immune and allergic response, cancer, and molecular signaling gene enrichment pathways. To infer causality, we performed bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and colocalization analyses. MR identified the expression of 8 genes as possibly causal for lipid levels; notable EEPD1 expression, linked with cellular cholesterol homeostasis, was inversely linked with TRIG levels. We also identified novel variants shared with LDL levels and gene expression of DDAH2, associated with cardiovascular disease, and TRIG level and expression of FCGRT, linked with maintaining triglyceride homeostasis. Phenome-wide enrichment analyses reported TRIG associated genes were enriched in secondary malignancy of bone suggesting broader systemic health implications of modified lipid levels. These findings highlight novel associations and genetic regulatory mechanisms as potential therapeutic targets for lipid dysregulation.

papers.title: Matrix Stiffness Controls Lipid Homeostasis in Human Corneal Endothelial Cells via a Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR-PPARγ Mechanotransduction Axis
papers.authors: Mingyue Zhong; Tingjun Fan; Jun Zhao
papers.abstract: Abstract Substrate stiffness is a critical mechanical cue that regulates cellular behaviors, yet its role in governing lipid homeostasis of human corneal endothelial cells (HCECs) remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a polyacrylamide hydrogel platform with tunable stiffnesses (25, 50, and 100 kPa) covering the pathophysiological range of Descemet’s membrane to investigate stiffness-dependent lipid metabolic reprogramming in HCECs. All hydrogels exhibited excellent transparency (>95%) and good biocompatibility. We found that soft substrates (25 kPa) promoted substantial accumulation of neutral lipids and free cholesterol in HCECs. Mechanistically, soft substrates upregulated SREBP1 and its target genes to enhance fatty acid synthesis while suppressing CPT1-mediated fatty acid oxidation, and simultaneously upregulated LDLR and SREBP2 to promote cholesterol uptake and synthesis while downregulating the LXRα-ABCA1/ABCG1 axis to impair cholesterol efflux. Notably, PPARγ emerged as a key regulator of stiffness-dependent lipid homeostasis; its expression was positively correlated with substrate stiffness, and pharmacological activation of PPARγ reversed soft substrate-induced lipid accumulation. Furthermore, the Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR signaling axis was identified as an upstream mechanotransduction pathway mediating stiffness-regulated PPARγ expression. Analysis of transcriptomic datasets from Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) patients revealed dysregulation of lipid metabolism genes consistent with our findings. Together, these results demonstrate that substrate stiffness governs HCEC lipid homeostasis through a Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR-PPARγ mechanotransduction cascade, and that matrix softening promotes abnormal lipid accumulation by reprogramming fatty acid and cholesterol metabolic networks. Our findings establish a mechanistic link between the mechanical microenvironment and lipid metabolism in corneal endothelial cells, providing insights into FECD pathogenesis and a theoretical framework for designing stiffness-tuned biomaterials for corneal endothelial regeneration.

papers.title: Stemonine Alleviates UVB‐Induced Keratinocyte Senescence by Activating SIRT3
papers.authors: Kun Chen; Xudong Yan; Guixiang You; Mingyang Li; Chen Chen; Xiaolan Yu; Jiyi Xia
papers.venue: Journal of Biochemical and Molecular Toxicology
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation is the primary environmental factor contributing to skin damage, largely by accelerating cellular senescence, which leads to impaired skin function and premature aging. Recent studies have indicated that Stemonine, a natural alkaloid, has therapeutic potential owing to its documented biological activities. In this study, we investigated the protective effects of Stemonine on immortalized human keratinocyte cell line HaCaT against UVB‐induced cellular senescence and elucidated the underlying mechanisms. Our results demonstrated that Stemonine significantly improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress, and ameliorated mitochondrial dysfunction in UVB‐irradiated HaCaT cells. Furthermore, Stemonine treatment reduced DNA damage signaling, downregulated key senescence executors such as acetylated p53 and p21, and decreased SA‐β‐Gal activity. Importantly, Stemonine upregulated both the expression and activity of SIRT3. Crucially, the protective effects of Stemonine were largely abolished upon SIRT3 knockdown, indicating that its actions are mediated via the SIRT3 pathway. These findings suggest that Stemonine is a promising candidate for mitigating UVB‐induced skin aging.

papers.title: Circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA and inflammation in Charcot-Marie-Tooth 1A and Charcot-Marie-Tooth 2A.
papers.authors: Zhenyu Li; Yize Li; Ping Li; Zhiying Xie; Meng Yu; Jianwen Deng; He Lv; Wei Zhang; Zhaoxia Wang; Lingchao Meng; Yun Yuan
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released from cells during such processes as mitophagy and apoptosis and can act as an endogenous damage-associated molecular pattern that activates innate immune responses. We investigated levels of circulating cell-free DNA (ccf-DNA), including ccf-mtDNA and circulating cell-free nuclear DNA (ccf-nDNA), and serum interleukin-1β (IL-1β) in patients with Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease, specifically with CMT1A and CMT2A. METHODS: This study enrolled 51 patients with CMT disease (42 with CMT1A and 9 with CMT2A, 31 males and 20 females) and 13 healthy controls (6 males and 7 females). The numbers of copies of serum ccf-mtDNA and ccf-nDNA, were quantified using ND1 and ACTB, respectively, before being measured via quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction. Serum IL-1β levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. The number of ccf-DNA copies, ND1/ACTB ratio, and IL-1β levels were compared between the three groups. And the correlation analysis was performed. RESULTS: Serum ND1 levels were higher in patients with CMT1A (p < 0.01) and CMT2A (p < 0.001) than in healthy controls, so was the ND1/ACTB ratio in the CMT1A (p < 0.001) and CMT2A (p < 0.05) groups. Serum IL-1β levels were higher in patients with CMT1A (p < 0.01) and CMT2A (p < 0.001) than in healthy controls. The ND1/ACTB ratio was positively related to the number of onion bulbs in CMT2A. No significant differences in serum ACTB, ND1, ND1/ACTB, or IL-1β levels were observed between the CMT1A and CMT2A groups. CONCLUSION: Patients with CMT1A and CMT2A had higher levels of serum ccf-mtDNA and IL-1β than in healthy controls. These findings suggest association between increased circulating mitochondrial DNA and inflammation in CMT disease. However, no subtype-specific differences were identified between CMT1A and CMT2A.

papers.title: Lipid Mediators and Metabolic Inflammation: From Molecular Mechanisms to a New Therapeutic Paradigm
papers.authors: Ivchuk V.
papers.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
papers.abstract: Chronic low-grade inflammation is a common pathogenetic mechanism of metabolic, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, and neurodegenerative diseases. This essay critically analyzes the role of lipid mediators in the pathogenesis of chronic inflammation and substantiates the thesis that the key factor in the transition from acute to chronic inflammation is not the excessive production of pro-inflammatory mediators, but the insufficiency of pro-resolution pathways. The molecular mechanisms of metabolic reprogramming of immune cells are reviewed, in particular, the switching of macrophages between glycolytic (M1) and oxidative (M2) phenotypes, the role of CD36 and FATP2 in lipotoxicity, impaired β-oxidation of fatty acids, and the accumulation of toxic lipid intermediates (free cholesterol, ceramides, lactate, succinate). The dual nature of lipid mediators is analyzed – from pro-inflammatory eicosanoids (LTB4, PGE2) to specialized pro-resolution mediators (SPMs), including lipoxins, resolvins, protectins and maresins. Data on the imbalance between pro-inflammatory and pro-resolution mediators in atherosclerosis, metabolic syndrome, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, neurodegenerative and autoimmune diseases are presented. Special attention is paid to the concept of “unalamation”, which radically rethinks the etiology of chronic inflammation. A therapeutic paradigm based on the stimulation of endogenous pro-resolution pathways (SPMs and their synthetic analogues) is substantiated as an alternative to traditional anti-inflammatory therapy that inhibits pro-inflammatory mediators. The limitations of existing research, controversies, and prospects for further scientific exploration in this field are discussed.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Lactate Signaling and Protein Lactylation in Neurological Diseases.
papers.authors: Yu Gu; Potao Zhang; Chunyan Lei; Wenyan Xu; Yunyu Cui
papers.abstract: The brain, as a highly metabolically active organ, depends on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to sustain energy demands. When mitochondrial function is impaired, cells undergo metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis, leading to lactate accumulation. Beyond its traditional role as a metabolic byproduct, lactate is now recognized as a signaling molecule that links metabolism to epigenetic regulation through protein lactylation, a post-translational modification identified by Zhang et al. in 2019. Research on lactylation has progressed through three stages: initial discovery in histone lactylation as an epigenetic mark, expansion to non-histone proteins revealing roles in metabolic and structural regulation, and recent identification of mitochondrial protein lactylation influencing OXPHOS, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. This review summarizes the mitochondrial-lactate-lactylation axis in the nervous system, including brain lactate metabolism, the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle, and regulatory mechanisms of lactylation (writers, erasers, and readers). We further discuss its roles in histone and non-histone modification, its bidirectional relationship with mitochondrial dysfunction, and its involvement in neurodegenerative, cerebrovascular, and neuropsychiatric disorders. Finally, we highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting lactylation pathways. Collectively, mitochondrial lactate signaling and protein lactylation emerge as a central link between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic dysregulation in neurological diseases, providing new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Maternal HFD and CDAHFD Exposure from Pregnancy to Lactation Differentially Affect Lipid Profiles and Behavior in Offspring Mice
papers.authors: Ryoken Aoki; Nobuo Izumo; Megumi Furukawa; Rena Ikeda; Chisato Takiya; Ayaka Ito; Hideo Matsuzaki
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Maternal nutritional status during pregnancy and lactation can influence metabolic and neurobehavioral development in offspring. However, the contribution of specific lipid alterations to these effects remains unclear. This study investigated whether maternal exposure to different high-fat diets produces distinct metabolic and neurobehavioral outcomes in offspring. Methods: Pregnant ICR mice were fed a control diet, a conventional high-fat diet (HFD), or a 50% choline-deficient, amino acid-defined high-fat diet (50% CDAHFD) from embryonic day 12 until weaning. Male offspring were assessed at 4–6 weeks of age for body weight, plasma lipid levels, behavioral phenotypes, prefrontal neurotransmitter release, and expression of genes related to serotonergic and dopaminergic signaling. A total of 31 dams and 196 offspring were used in the experiments and allocated to each experimental group. Results: Offspring in both HFD and 50% CDAHFD groups exhibited increased body weight and total cholesterol levels compared to controls, whereas plasma triglycerides were elevated a tendency in the 50% CDAHFD group. HFD offspring showed reduced spontaneous locomotor activity, and increased prefrontal serotonin release with altered serotonergic gene expression. Conversely, 50% CDAHFD offspring displayed increased exploratory behavior in the open field test alongside altered dopamine neuron-related genes, without locomotor or social deficits. Conclusions: Exposure of mothers to different high-fat diets has been suggested to cause specific changes in their offspring’s lipid profiles, which in turn modulate the serotonin and dopamine systems differently, leading to specific behavioral changes.

papers.title: Reversing amorphous aging associated with resistance drift in phase-change memory via atomistic rejuvenation
papers.authors: Kaiqi Li; Xuanguang Zhang; Jian Zhou; Bin Liu; Zhimei Sun
papers.abstract: Resistance drift in the amorphous RESET state limits phase-change memory (PCM) for multilevel storage and neuromorphic computing. Most mitigation strategies slow the drift rather than reverse the structural aging that develops after programming. Here, we use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with a Y–Sb–Te neuroevolution potential to examine atomistic rejuvenation in Sb–Te-based glasses. Aging and rejuvenation are quantified using potential energy, radial distribution functions, global Steinhardt order parameters, ring statistics, and homopolar bonding, which track short-range relaxation, topological ordering, and bond rearrangement. Binary Sb–Te models first establish competing thermal pathways: low-temperature annealing promotes energetic relaxation and ordering, whereas high-temperature reheating followed by requenching restores higher-energy, less-aged amorphous states while avoiding prolonged residence in the crystallization-prone window. In Y-doped Sb2Te3, Y reduces energetic relaxation, delays four-membered-ring ordering, and reduces bonding fluctuations while preserving reversible rejuvenation. Device-scale simulations further show that rejuvenation pulses reset key aging-sensitive descriptors in a 6.5 × 105-atom mushroom-cell PCM model. These results demonstrate that atomistic rejuvenation can reverse aging-sensitive structural features in Sb–Te-based PCM glasses, providing a structural route toward mitigating resistance drift.

papers.title: The senescence-linked factor Chi3L1 contributes to mesenchymal stromal cells dysfunction promoting joint aging and osteoarthritis progression
papers.authors: Maroun G, Bonnefont A, Silva R, Terreza C, Pradenas C, Asencio C, Robert B, De Seny D, De CEUNINCK F, Pastoureau P, Jorgensen C, Djouad F, Pers Y, Brondello J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Ageing progressively disrupts joint homeostasis and increases susceptibility to osteoarthritis (OA), yet why repair fails in the altered joint remains poorly understood. Cellular senescence accumulates with age and is prominent in osteoarthritic joints, contributing to a persistent catabolic, inflammatory and tissue-remodelling microenvironment through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Such signals can alter the function of endogenous reparative cells including mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), which are important to tissue repair and immunomodulation. Nonetheless, little is known on which senescence associated stromal factors within this altered niche could compromise MSCs competence. In this study, we are interested by chitinase-3-like 1 (CHI3L1), a SASP glycoprotein whose levels are elevated in both ageing and OA. We revealed that CHI3L1 accumulates in OA joints in correlation with senescence and the disease features, where it in vitro chronic exposure converts MSC toward a dysfunctional age-like state characterized by impaired potencies, disrupted tri-lineage commitment, reduced mobility, altered metabolomic profiling, loss of immunomodulatory activity together with an acquisition of a pro-inflammatory secretome. Consequently, CHI3L1 preconditioning abolishes the homeostatic function of healthy MSCs in an inflammatory OA model. Conversely, in spontaneous age-related OA model, MSC transplantation combined to CHI3L1 transient neutralization restores joint dynamics by enhancing cartilage repair, reducing synovial inflammation, preventing bone remodeling, improving maximal speed locomotor and shifting selective circulated factors related to stromal, skeletal, and hematopoietic homeostasis toward a more youthful pattern. Collectively, our findings establish CHI3L1 as a novel senescence-associated contributor in the decline of MSC fitness and regenerative niche competence during joint ageing. Furthermore, it provides a rationale for combining microenvironment-targeted interventions with stem cell therapy to maximize their potentials for tissue regeneration in age-related diseases.

papers.title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia Aggravates the Pyroptosis of Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells Through Regulating Mitophagy‐Mediated NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation
papers.authors: Yuwei Zhang; Hongyan Tai
papers.venue: Journal of Biochemical and Molecular Toxicology
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)‐induced renal injury is triggered by chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Our previous article has revealed that CIH triggers the pyroptosis of renal tubular epithelial cells through the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, whereas the mechanism by which CIH activates NLRP3 inflammasome remains elusive. Rats and HK‐2 cells were exposed to CIH to establish CIH models. Histopathological staining, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine (Scr) levels were examined to assess renal injury. Western blot and immunofluorescence assay were used to assess proteins related to NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptosis and mitophagy. Mitochondrial membrane potential and production of ROS and ATP were examined to evaluate mitochondrial function. CCK‐8, LDH release and ELISA assays were performed to assess cell injury and inflammation. Mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi‐1) was applied for a rescue assay. CIH induced renal injury and suppressed mitophagy in vivo, evidenced by worsening pathological features, elevated Scr and BUN levels, reduced colocalization of Tom20 with LC3B, and downregulated expression of LC3‐II/I ratio, Atg5, PINK1 and Parkin. PINK1 overexpression restored mitophagy by enhancing colocalization of mitochondria with LC3B, upregulating LC3‐II/I ratio and Atg5, and restored mitochondrial function of CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells through enhancing mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing ROS production and increasing ATP content. PINK1 overexpression alleviated cell viability, inflammation and NLRP3 inflammasome‐mediated pyroptosis in CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells, which were partly abolished by Mdivi‐1. PINK1 attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome‐mediated pyroptosis in CIH‐exposed HK‐2 cells partially through restoring mitophagy and mitochondrial function, providing potential therapeutic strategies for OSA‐related kidney diseases.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture Alleviates Chemotherapy- Associated Cancer-Related Fatigue by Restoring Mitochondrial Homeostasis.
papers.authors: Shiyin Lie; Xi Xiao; Miaomiao Xu; Jingchun Zeng; Liming Lu; Jietao Lin
papers.abstract: ObjectiveCancer-related fatigue (CRF) is a persistent and debilitating symptom commonly associated with cancer cachexia and impaired physical function, yet effective therapeutic strategies remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the anti-fatigue effects of electroacupuncture (EA) and to explore its underlying mechanisms.MethodsA CRF mouse model was established by 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) administration. EA was applied at ST36. Fatigue-related behaviors were assessed using rotarod, grip strength, swimming, and open-field tests. Skeletal muscle morphology was evaluated by histological staining, and mitochondrial ultrastructure was examined by transmission electron microscopy. Mitochondrial function and oxidative stress were assessed by measuring membrane potential (ΔΨm), mtDNA content, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity. The expression of mitochondrial dynamics-related genes was analyzed by RT-qPCR.ResultsEA significantly alleviated fatigue-like behaviors, improving muscle strength, endurance, and locomotor activity in CRF mice. EA preserved muscle fiber morphology and increased cross-sectional area. Mitochondrial structural damage induced by 5-FU was markedly attenuated by EA. Furthermore, EA restored mitochondrial membrane potential and mtDNA content, reduced ROS levels, and enhanced SOD activity. The dysregulated expression of mitochondrial dynamics-related genes was also normalized by EA.ConclusionsEA can alleviate CRF by regulating mitochondrial dynamics and reducing oxidative stress in skeletal muscle, highlighting its potential as a novel intervention for CRF treatment.

papers.title: Urolithin A Attenuates Noise-induced Hearing Loss and Is Associated With Increased Cochlear Mitophagy Markers
papers.authors: SUNG IL CHO; EU-RI JO; JEONGHYUN OH
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is a prevalent cause of sensorineural hearing impairment, in which mitochondrial dysfunction plays a key pathogenic role. Mitophagy is essential for maintaining mitochondrial quality control. This study investigated whether urolithin A (UA), a known mitophagy inducer, protects against NIHL. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight-week-old CBA/J mice were divided into three groups: control, noise + saline, and noise + UA (10 mg/kg). NIHL was induced by exposure to broadband noise (100 dB SPL, 2 h). UA was administered intraperitoneally before and after noise exposure. Auditory function was evaluated using auditory brainstem response (ABR). Mitophagy-associated markers and mitochondrial function were assessed by Western blotting, quantitative real-time PCR, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) integrity analysis, ATP measurements, and immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence. RESULTS: UA treatment significantly reduced auditory threshold shifts compared with the untreated group. The expression levels of mitophagy-related proteins and genes, including PINK1, Parkin, and BNIP3, were significantly increased in the UA-treated group. In addition, UA restored ATP levels following noise exposure. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analyses demonstrated enhanced formation of mitophagosomes and mitophagolysosomes in the cochlea, including the organ of Corti and the spiral ganglion, in the UA-treated group. CONCLUSION: UA attenuates NIHL by enhancing mitophagy-associated markers and preserving mitochondrial function in the cochlea. These findings suggest that pharmacological activation of mitophagy may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for NIHL.

papers.title: Biological State-Space and Adaptive Reserve Across Scales: An Entropy-Symmetry Framework for Ageing and Cancer
papers.authors: Peacock EJ.
papers.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
papers.abstract: Biological function depends on constrained transitions between physiological states, yet a biomarker sampled at a single time point describes only an occupied state, not the pathways accessible from it; capacity to respond, recover or tolerate further challenge is inferred accordingly. To address this distinction, a framework drawing on concepts of entropy and symmetry is postulated, in which molecular, structural, energetic, immune, and temporal constraints shape the integrity of the occupied state and access to a repertoire of viable states.A symmetry-integrity function, Φ(t), serves as a latent descriptor of a currently occupied multiscale state. Adaptive reserve describes the breadth, connectivity, traversability and recoverability of viable state-space; resilience defines its effective deployment during perturbation. Ordinary physiological capacity is distinguished from failsafe responses, through which unresolved burden may be contained or damaged components eliminated while higher-order function is sustained. Such compensation can preserve current output despite restricted transitions, maintenance expenditures and reduced capacity to absorb subsequent challenges. Physiological and failsafe responses may draw on pre-existing capacity and challenge-induced mechanisms.In this context, ageing is hypothesised to alter state accessibility through loss of viable states, altered transition barriers, slower restoration, increased stochastic dispersion in state-space or pathological trapping. Cancer presents a nested-scale problem in which malignant reserve can be preserved while constraints that sustain host function deteriorate. Quiescence, reproductive transitions and comparative longevity illustrate the distinction between contemporaneous activity, integrity of the occupied state and retained response capacity.An operational schema is developed using spatially specified measurements, graded perturbations, recovery dynamics and repeated challenges. Membrane organisation, multivariate molecular profiles and spatial tumour states afford candidate descriptions of occupied states, with measured states distinguished from inferred trajectories. Testable predictions concern compensated function, activation thresholds, response ceilings and whether niche context adds predictive information. The framework is a testable synthesis whose explanatory and predictive value lies in its assessment against simpler models based on baseline state, damage burden and recovery. It gives a basis for subsequent evaluation of therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Cellular Senescence in Diabetic Kidney Disease: Mechanisms and Treatments
papers.authors: Yudian Wang; Yufei Zhang; Di Niu; Yuyan Fan; Yachan Gao; Xinxin Pang; Qi Jin
papers.venue: Integrative Medicine in Nephrology and Andrology
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence refers to a state of stable and essentially irreversible cell cycle arrest, accompanied by extensive changes in cellular secretory activity. Senescent cells accumulate within tissues during physiological aging and in response to various forms of cellular stress or injury. While transient senescence is essential for processes such as embryonic development, tissue regeneration, and tumor suppression, the persistent retention of senescent cells has been increasingly recognized as a key driver of aging and age-related diseases. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD), a prevalent chronic complication of diabetes, is characterized by accelerated renal cellular senescence and progressive accumulation of senescent cells, both of which contribute to structural damage and functional deterioration of the kidney. These observations have positioned cellular senescence as a promising therapeutic target for slowing the onset and progression of DKD. This review summarizes the fundamental characteristics and major classifications of cellular senescence; discusses its physiological and pathological functions, together with the underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms; examines the role of senescence in renal cell injury during DKD progression, and highlights recent advances in senescence-targeted therapeutic strategies for DKD.

papers.title: Impact of SPAK Deficiency on Glomerular Injury and Mitochondrial Homeostasis in Adriamycin-Induced FSGS
papers.authors: CHIEN-WEI HUANG; HSIN-HUNG CHEN; JIN-SHUEN CHEN
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is characterized by podocyte injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic remodeling. STE20/SPS1-related proline-alanine-rich kinase (SPAK), a downstream component of WNK signaling, regulates renal ion transport and has been implicated in inflammatory and stress responses. This study examined the impact of SPAK deficiency on renal injury and mitochondrial homeostasis in Adriamycin-induced FSGS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight-week-old male wild-type and global SPAK knockout C57BL/6 mice received a single intravenous injection of Adriamycin (18 mg/kg) or saline and were followed for four weeks. Renal function, proteinuria, glomerular histology, podocyte markers, mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and targeted metabolic profiles were assessed using biochemical assays, histology, immunohistochemistry, TUNEL staining, western blotting, quantitative PCR, and LC-MS-based metabolomics. RESULTS: Adriamycin induced proteinuria, serum creatinine elevation, glomerulosclerosis, and reduced nephrin and podocin expression in both wild-type and SPAK knockout mice. The severity of renal functional and histological injury was comparable between the two FSGS groups. SPAK deficiency was associated with baseline mitochondrial and apoptotic abnormalities, including reduced ATP5A1 expression and increased TUNEL-positive cells. In FSGS kidneys, SPAK deficiency did not restore ATP5A1, OPA1, PGC-1α, redox balance, or glycolytic remodeling, and SPAK-knockout FSGS mice exhibited greater apoptosis than wild-type FSGS mice. CONCLUSION: SPAK deficiency modifies mitochondrial and apoptotic responses but does not attenuate Adriamycin-induced glomerular injury. These findings suggest that SPAK contributes to glomerular homeostasis and that its role in kidney injury is context-dependent.

papers.title: Lactobacillus johnsonii attenuates ovarian aging by remodeling the gut–ovary axis
papers.authors: Jiamin He; Qiwen Wang; Luyi Chen; Yadong Qi; Dingjiacheng Jia; Jilei Xu; Qingyi Wang; Yao Jiang; Jian Zhou; Yong Sun; Ruochen Yan; Lan Wang; Tongyao Hou; Zheng Kuang; Min Jin; Liangjing Wang; Shujie Chen
papers.abstract: Abstract Reproductive aging, accompanied by abnormal levels of sex hormones, affects overall health and poses a particular threat to women. Gut microbiota plays a key role in regulating host aging and is promising for alleviating reproductive aging. Here, we found that gut commensal Lactobacillus johnsonii ( L. johnsonii ) declined in accordance with ovarian failure in female aging mice. Restoring L. johnsonii partially rescued hormone levels in age‐ or chemically‐ induced ovarian decline murine models, thereby reversing cognitive decline and extending lifespan. Indole‐3‐propionic acid (IPA), the bioactive metabolite of L. johnsonii , promoted granulosa cell proliferation to upregulate sex‐steroid output by activating the AhR‐YAP signaling pathway. L. johnsonii ‐derived LdhA was identified as the essential enzyme for indole‐3‐lactic acid (ILA) biosynthesis, thereby increasing downstream IPA. In addition, significant positive correlations were observed between ovarian function and fecal L. johnsonii , as well as IPA levels. These findings establish L. johnsonii as a promising probiotic strategy for alleviating ovarian aging through microbiota‐derived metabolite signaling along the gut–ovary axis.

papers.title: Membrane Diffusion Mode of Human Perforin-1 and Its Cholesterol Sensitivity.
papers.authors: Yuri Kasubuchi; Ryuhei Harada
papers.venue: The journal of physical chemistry. B
papers.abstract: Perforin-1, a pore-forming protein, is essential for cytotoxic T lymphocyte- and natural killer cell-mediated immune responses. Human perforin-1 (hPRF) exists as a surface-bound monomer that diffuses on the membrane before oligomerizing into a prepore complex. Yet this diffusive stage evades direct experimental observation, and how cholesterol regulates hPRF mobility remains unknown. We therefore performed all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the hPRF monomer on lipid membranes with 0-60 mol % cholesterol to identify which lipid environments support or hinder efficient hPRF diffusion. The lateral diffusion coefficient of hPRF decreased progressively with cholesterol content, tracking reduced area per lipid up to 40 mol %. Beyond this packing-saturation point, the hPRF diffusion continued to slow, suggesting a contribution from direct protein-lipid interactions. Intermolecular contact analysis identified W431 and F432 as persistent cholesterol-binding sites that drive raft-like codiffusion of hPRF with an ordered lipid assembly rather than independent diffusion. These results demonstrate that cholesterol suppresses hPRF lateral dynamics through both indirect membrane ordering and direct, residue-specific protein-lipid local interactions, providing molecular-level insights into the early stages of perforin-mediated cytotoxicity. This dual mechanism suggests that, beyond limiting hPRF binding, cholesterol-rich effector-cell membranes may also suppress its lateral diffusion, providing an additional layer of self-protection from perforin-mediated lysis.

papers.title: Neurovascular-immune-clearance remodeling in brain aging
papers.authors: Yuxin Liu; Ronghao Yang; Haocai Chang
papers.abstract: Brain aging involves concurrent changes in cerebral vessels, immune regulation, and waste clearance, yet these processes are often studied separately. This fragmented approach limits understanding of how dysfunction in one system influences the others and contributes to age-related neurological disorders. This review summarizes current evidence on the neurovascular-immune-clearance axis, focusing on neurovascular unit deterioration, impaired glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic transport, neuroimmune remodeling, and the cell-specific mechanisms that connect these processes. We further compare their shared and disease-dependent roles in Alzheimer’s disease, vascular cognitive impairment, and late-life depression. Available imaging, fluid, proteomic, and epigenetic biomarkers are evaluated for their ability to measure different components of this axis, and emerging interventions are organized according to their predominant effects on vascular support, clearance function, immune signaling, and cellular senescence. Current evidence indicates that brain aging is characterized by interacting and partially compensable functional bottlenecks rather than a single linear pathological pathway. Integrating these mechanisms provides a framework for interpreting heterogeneous aging phenotypes, selecting complementary biomarkers, and developing mechanism-guided interventions. Future progress will depend on longitudinal human validation and direct demonstration that target engagement produces durable neurological benefit.

papers.title: Perturbation of Melatonin Signaling Modulates Respiration and Mitochondrial Gene Expression in Arabidopsis thaliana During Photooxidative Stress
papers.authors: I. A. Bychkov; N. A. Shugaeva; A. G. Shugaev; N. V. Kudryakova; V. V. Kusnetsov
papers.abstract: Abstract Melatonin (MT) is a critical regulator of mitochondria that affects bioenergetics, dynamics, and gene expression, and effectively protects them from oxidative stress. In this study we elucidated the role of the putative melatonin receptor CAND2/PMTR1 in mitochondrial respiration and the melatonin-mediated expression of mitochondrial genes under high light (HL) stress. Disruption of CAND2 and its associated partner GPA1 in Arabidopsis thaliana resulted in an increase in the respiration rate predominantly due to cytochrome respiration (CP), in contrast to wild type (WT) plants and 35SCAND2 overexpressing line in which an increase of alternative respiration (AP) prevails. MT treatment decreased AP activation under HL and reduced the overall leaf respiration rate, however, these effects were less pronounced in cand2 and gpa1 mutants. Increase in an AP capacity under HL stress positively correlated with an increase in transcript accumulation of the alternative oxidase (AOX) genes ( AOX1a , AOX1d ). At the same time, under stress conditions, the expression of the studied CP genes ( cob, cox1 ) and the ATPase gene ( atp6-1 ) was suppressed. MT treatment completely removed this inhibition, but only in WT and 35SCAND2 plants. Moreover, cand2 showed elevated steady state transcript levels of genes associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, suggesting an initial stress state of the mutant. The effects of exogenous melatonin on mitochondrial gene activity were mainly dependent on CAND2 receptor activity, although some genes were regulated by melatonin independently of CAND2, indicating the multiple mechanisms of melatonin perception in plants. Thus, disruption of MT signaling has a significant impact on mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial gene expression.

papers.title: Prognostic significance of SLC25A28 and its associations with mitochondrial metabolism and immune features in glioma
papers.authors: Wangyang Yu; Yue Yang; Wenli Guo; Yafeng Wang; Jinsong Bai; Chen Li
papers.abstract: Background SLC25A28 encodes the mitochondrial iron transporter mitoferrin-2, but its prognostic relevance and biological associations in glioma remain incompletely characterized. We investigated its clinical significance and relationships with metabolic, ferroptosis-related and immune features across glioma cohorts. Methods SLC25-family genes were screened in CGGA and TCGA, followed by survival analysis and meta-analysis across nine GlioVis cohorts. Clinical Cox models, prognostic scores and grade/IDH subgroups were evaluated. Metabolic, immune and curated ferroptosis-related signatures were examined using clinically adjusted models, and immune-cell and checkpoint analyses underwent false-discovery-rate correction. SLC25A28 expression was assessed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting. Results Lower SLC25A28 expression was associated with unfavorable clinicopathological features and shorter overall survival (pooled hazard ratio, 1.91; 95% confidence interval, 1.46–2.50; I² = 84.9%). Exploratory analyses supported survival associations in both IDH-mutant and IDH-wild-type subgroups of CGGA and TCGA, although findings within glioblastoma varied. Positive oxidative-phosphorylation associations persisted after grade/IDH adjustment in both pooled cohorts; within glioblastoma, this association was supported in CGGA but not TCGA. Ferroptosis-related transcriptional associations were also detected, with consistent all-glioma WikiPathways results across sensitivity analyses in TCGA but scoring-method and cohort dependence in regulator signatures. Immune-cell differences survived correction for 10 of 22 populations in CGGA and 16 of 22 in TCGA, and three checkpoint genes showed positive correlations in both cohorts. qRT-PCR and Western blotting confirmed lower SLC25A28 expression in U87 and U251 cells than in normal human astrocytes. Conclusions SLC25A28 is a candidate prognostic biomarker associated with mitochondrial metabolism, ferroptosis-related transcriptional features and immune features in glioma. Multi-cohort survival evidence and clinically adjusted molecular associations support further evaluation of its prognostic and biological relevance. Subtype-specific clinical validation and functional investigations will help define its clinical utility and biological role.
