papers.title: Purpurin Alleviates Meniscal Senescence and Osteoarthritis by Blocking the Non‐Metabolic Function of Hexokinase 2
papers.authors: Zhencan Lin; Ming Li; Wei Li; Tianfa Xu; Zongrui Jiang; Yanlin Zhong; Aishan He; Xiaoyi Zhao; Dianbo Long; Yan Kang
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Meniscal degeneration, characterised by extracellular matrix (ECM) loss and cellular senescence, plays a critical role in osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Although hexokinase 2 (HK2) is recognised as a key glycolytic enzyme, its potential non‐metabolic functions in the meniscus remain unexplored. In this study, HK2 expression was evaluated in human OA and normal meniscus tissues, and its non‐metabolic effects were investigated in primary meniscal cells using overexpression, knockdown, and site‐directed mutagenesis; protein interactions were analysed by immunoprecipitation‐mass spectrometry (IP‐MS) and co‐immunoprecipitation (Co‐IP). HK2 was significantly upregulated in OA meniscal tissues, and overexpression of catalytically inactive HK2 promoted meniscal ECM degradation and cellular senescence in an MYH10‐dependent manner. Mechanistically, HK2 enhanced the MYH10–PRKN interaction, inducing K48‐linked ubiquitination of MYH10 at lysine 410 and its subsequent proteasomal degradation, thereby reducing COL1A1 mRNA stability. Purpurin, identified through virtual screening, disrupted the HK2–MYH10 interaction in vitro, prevented MYH10 degradation, and attenuated cellular senescence. In the destabilisation of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model, intra‐articular injection of adeno‐associated virus expressing catalytically inactive HK2 exacerbated OA progression, whereas purpurin treatment alleviated meniscal degeneration, ECM loss, and OA‐associated pain. Collectively, HK2 promotes meniscal senescence and OA progression through a non‐metabolic, MYH10‐dependent mechanism, and purpurin represents a promising lead compound for disease‐modifying osteoarthritis drug (DMOAD) development.

papers.title: Toxic Concentrations of Glutamate Induce Ferroptosis without Affecting Mitochondrial Respiration in Rodent Brain Slice Cultures.
papers.authors: Annette Vaglio-Garro; Marco Theuermann; Katharina E Sweis; Sergejs Zavadskis; Márton Kokas; Zsuzsanna Környei; Miriam Karas; Laszlo Tretter; Tímea Komlódi; Adelheid Weidinger; Andrey V Kozlov
papers.abstract: Many neuronal disorders are characterized by glutamate toxicity, which is closely associated with mitochondrial and neuronal dysfunction. The aim of this study was to investigate the link between mitochondrial function and mechanisms of cell death induced by glutamate. The study was carried out on male (C57BL/6) mice and male Sprague Dawley rat acute brain slices (ABSs), as well as male and female organotypic brain slice cultures (BSCs). Mitochondrial respiration, activities of tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, and the cell death rate [assessed by lactate dehydrogenase release and histological analyses] were determined. Memantine was used to inhibit excitotoxicity, while ferrostatin-1, rosiglitazone, and deferoxamine were used as inhibitors of the ferroptotic pathway. In astrocytes, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (OGDHC) showed <1% of the enzymatic activity observed in the whole-brain tissue. In BSCs, glutamate exposure induced a marked increase in oxidative phosphorylation-linked mitochondrial respiration, which was independent of OGDHC activity and disappeared when BSC homogenates were analyzed. Glutamate-induced cell death was not alleviated by memantine but was significantly reduced by ferrostatin-1. The activation of ferroptosis by glutamate was also observed in ABSs, as well as the inhibition of lipid peroxidation induced by ferrostatin-1, rosiglitazone, and deferoxamine. Ferrostatin-1 and rosiglitazone additionally inhibited cell death, while deferoxamine did not. The unusual response to deferoxamine requires further elucidation. In summary, our data suggest that elevated glutamate levels enhance neuronal energy metabolism in brain slices, compensating glutamate-mediated Ca2+ influx and reduce excitotoxicity. In contrast, persistently elevated levels of extracellular glutamate impair the cystine/glutamate antiporter, leading to ferroptosis.

papers.title: Beyond Mitochondrial Fission: Emerging Roles of Drp1 in Skeletal Muscle Physiology and Disease
papers.authors: Kai Zou; Nicolas J. Berger; Zhenqi Zhou; Benjamin A. Kugler
papers.abstract: Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is best recognized as the primary regulator of mitochondrial fission. However, emerging evidence indicates that Drp1 is a multifaceted regulator of skeletal muscle physiology whose functions extend well beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial fission. Recent studies have identified novel roles of Drp1 in regulating substrate utilization, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species signaling, respiratory complex assembly, and mitochondrial-to-nuclear signaling, including mechanisms independent of its canonical fission activity. Importantly, Drp1 regulation in skeletal muscle is highly context-dependent, as both excessive and insufficient Drp1 activity can disrupt skeletal muscle homeostasis. For example, excessive Drp1 activation and mitochondrial fragmentation are associated with insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and neuromuscular diseases, whereas severe or prolonged Drp1 deficiency impairs mitochondrial quality control, bioenergetics, induce muscle atrophy, and compromise the exercise training adaptations. Therefore, the biological consequences of Drp1 modulation are highly context dependent and influenced by the metabolic and physiological state of skeletal muscle. In this review, we summarize the molecular regulation and emerging functions of Drp1 in skeletal muscle, with particular emphasis on fission-independent mechanisms and Drp1 dysregulation in metabolic and neuromuscular diseases. We further discuss pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies for modulating Drp1 signaling and highlight emerging approaches for skeletal muscle-specific targeting. Collectively, current evidence supports a paradigm in which skeletal muscle Drp1 functions as a multifaceted regulator of mitochondrial and skeletal muscle homeostasis, highlighting the therapeutic potential of modulating Drp1 activity to optimize mitochondrial and muscle health across different physiological and pathological contexts.

papers.title: Huaier Attenuates Renal Injury in Type 2 Diabetic Nephropathy by Ameliorating Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Inhibiting Tubular Epithelial Cell Apoptosis
papers.authors: Yucan Guan; Xiaoying Bai; Xianping Wei; Tao Ding; Ping Luo; Ping Nie
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a major microvascular complication of Type 2 diabetes, with renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs) apoptosis playing a pivotal role in its progression. The aqueous extract of Trametes robiniophila Murr. (Huaier) has shown renoprotective effects, but its specific molecular mechanisms in DN remain to be fully elucidated. Objective This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic effects of Huaier aqueous extract on DN and verify whether its anti‐apoptotic mechanism is mediated through the Wnt/β‐catenin pathway using the pathway activator SKL2001. Methods In vivo, KKAy Type 2 diabetic mice were treated with Huaier (5 g/kg/day) for 12 weeks to evaluate renal function and histopathology. In vitro, HK‐2 cells were treated with high glucose and palmitate (HG + PA) to induce injury. The Wnt/β‐catenin pathway activator SKL2001 was employed to determine if activating this pathway could abolish the protective effects of Huaier. Results Bioinformatics analysis indicates that the regulation of apoptosis is the primary mechanism by which Huaier improves DN. In vivo, Huaier reduced UACR and improved renal histopathology in KKAy mice. Consistently, TUNEL staining and molecular analysis confirmed that Huaier significantly suppressed RTECs apoptosis within the renal tissues. In vitro experiments demonstrated that Huaier significantly inhibited HG + PA‐induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and RTECs apoptosis. Notably, the administration of SKL2001 effectively reversed these protective effects, leading to increased β‐catenin expression and elevated apoptosis levels despite Huaier treatment. Conclusion Huaier aqueous extract mitigates RTECs apoptosis and renal injury in Type 2 diabetic nephropathy by suppressing the Wnt5a/β‐catenin signaling pathway.

papers.title: JWA as a context-dependent redox regulatory hub linking stress responses with aging hallmarks and age-related diseases
papers.authors: Yaning Wu; Ning Zhang; Hui Sun; Heng Fang; Guangli Yan; Xijun Wang
papers.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
papers.abstract: JWA (also known as ARL6IP5) is an evolutionarily conserved multifunctional protein increasingly implicated in redox homeostasis and cellular stress adaptation. Its functions intersect with redox homeostasis through signaling pathways including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), and adenosine 5′-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), as well as interactions with key proteins such as X-ray repair cross-complementing 1 (XRCC1), nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4), and excitatory amino acid carrier 1 (EAAC1) involved in oxidative-stress adaptation. As a redox-responsive regulatory protein and mediator, JWA exhibits context-dependent roles in disease pathogenesis: in oncology, it acts as a tumor suppressor by mitigating oxidative stress-induced DNA damage and reversing chemoresistance, with reduced expression correlating with poor prognosis in gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and other malignancies; in neurobiology, it exerts neuroprotective effects through suppression of ferroptosis, regulation of glutamate homeostasis, and proteostasis-related mechanisms, with the strength and direction of redox involvement varying across experimental contexts; beyond these fields, JWA regulates intestinal barrier integrity, radiation response, and adaptation to environmental oxidants (Cd, B [a]P, H 2 O 2 ), while specific polymorphisms influence redox-related disease susceptibility. As a potential aging-associated regulator, accumulating evidence suggests that JWA expression or activity may change during aging, although age-, tissue-, and disease-specific patterns remain incompletely defined. Current evidence links JWA dysregulation to oxidative stress and tissue dysfunction in several age-associated diseases, whereas its direct roles in the aging process remain insufficiently established. This review, centered on redox regulation as the unifying framework, comprehensively synthesizes current knowledge on JWA’s multifunctional roles across disciplines, highlights its potential as a candidate redox-related biomarker and experimental therapeutic target, and proposes an evidence-based research framework for future investigation and translation. By emphasizing JWA’s role in maintaining redox balance and its regulatory function in aging process and age-related diseases, we provide novel insights into its significance in future clinical-development considerations and offer directions for targeting redox dysregulation in refractory diseases.

papers.title: Mechanical stress-induced release of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA activates RIG-I to drive osteogenic differentiation in aortic disease
papers.authors: Graef, M.; Bender, F.; Dudek, S.; Vasileiadou, P.; Soler, S.; Schlee-Guimaraes, T. M.; Steinheuer, L. M.; Spitzer, J.; Thurley, K.; Nowak, R. P.; Maser, K.; Schmidt, S.; Goody, P. R.; Schlee, M.; Zimmer, S.; Nickenig, G.; Zillinger, T.; Bartok, E.; Hartmann, G.
papers.abstract: Background: Gain-of-function mutations in RIG-I and MDA5 (RIG-I-like receptors, RLR) cause Singleton-Merten syndrome, an interferonopathy with early aortic calcification. Here we set out to study a possible involvement of RIG-I-like receptor signaling in the formation of aortic valve stenosis in general. Methods and results: We investigated whether mechanical stress-induced RLR activation promotes osteogenic differentiation and calcification of primary human aortic cells, whether such RLR activation drives the development of aortic valve stenosis in vivo, and whether inhibition of downstream JAK/STAT activation ameliorates aortic valve stenosis. We found that activation of primary human aortic interstitial cells by exogenous RIG-I- and MDA5 agonists induced a type I interferon response and an osteogenic program including increased expression of BMP-2 and BSP2, and promoted calcification. These effects were RIG-I/MDA5 or MAVS-dependent, as assessed by CRISPR/Cas9 knockouts. The stress-granule protein G3BP1 and the Wnt receptor FZD5 were induced downstream of RLR activation and were required for osteogenic gene expression and calcification. To assess a potential endogenous source of RIG-I activation, mechanical stretch mimicking valvular tissue stress was applied in cell cuture, which induced a significant RIG-I-dependent interferon response. Sequencing of highly purified preparations of double-stranded RNA from stretched cells demonstrated a predominant mitochondrial origin of double-stranded RNA, and depleting mitochondrial RNA abolished the stretch-dependent response. The JAK/STAT inhibitor ruxolitinib suppressed the RIG-I-induced response including the expression of osteogenic factors in vitro. In a murine wire-injury model of aortic stenosis, MAVS deficiency attenuated valvular morphological changes and improved hemodynamic parameters. Ruxolitinib attenuated hemodynamic progression, prevented aortic stenosis development, and improved survival. Conclusions: Altogether, our results demonstrate that the mechanical-stress-induced release of mitochondrial double-stranded RNA activates RIG-I signaling in aortic interstitial cells, thereby driving osteogenic differentiation and calcification via a MAVS- and G3BP1-dependent pathway. JAK/STAT inhibition with ruxolitinib mitigates this process in a mouse model of aortic valve stenosis, identifying a candidate therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α signaling pathway: Molecular mechanisms from mitochondrial function regulation to the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases
papers.authors: Miaoyan Tang; Jing Miao
papers.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial dysfunction is considered a central factor in the onset and progression of various neurodegenerative diseases. Sirtuin 1 is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-dependent deacetylase that senses changes in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide/reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide ratio and activates the transcriptional coactivator peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α through deacetylation. Activated peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α subsequently interacts with multiple transcription factors to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, mitochondrial dynamics, autophagy, energy metabolism, and antioxidant defense, thereby playing a critical role in maintaining mitochondrial functional homeostasis. Preclinical studies have shown that neurodegenerative diseases are frequently accompanied by downregulation of the expression or activity of key components of the Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α pathway, whereas activation of this pathway can ameliorate associated mitochondrial dysfunction and exert neuroprotective effects. This article systematically elucidates the pivotal role of the Sirtuin 1/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α pathway in neurodegenerative diseases from the perspectives of molecular structure, interaction mechanisms, and regulation of mitochondrial function, aiming to provide a theoretical foundation for the development of novel multi-target drugs and intervention strategies.

papers.title: Beyond Glycemic Control: The Pleiotropic Role of GLP-1RAs and Melatonin in Combating Neuroinflammation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
papers.authors: Reiter RJ, Sharma R, Simão VA, Chuffa LGdA, Carloni S, Gentile C, Balduini W, Manucha W.
papers.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and impaired protein homeostasis form interconnected pathological networks in acute central nervous system injury and chronic neurodegenerative disease. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), originally developed for metabolic disorders, exhibit neuroprotective activity in experimental models through effects on neuronal survival, metabolic adaptation, and inflammatory signaling. Melatonin complements these actions through mitochondrial redox protection, preservation of bioenergetics, and circadian regulation. This narrative review examines the pharmacological diversity and central nervous system accessibility of GLP-1RAs, including emerging multi-receptor agonists, and their convergence with melatonin on AMPK, sirtuin–PGC-1α, and mitochondrial quality-control networks. Evidence from stroke, traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and type 2 diabetes-associated cognitive decline highlights opportunities to translate these mechanisms into neuroprotective strategies. Experimental efficacy, exploratory cognitive findings, and existing clinical experience provide a foundation for further investigation, while heterogeneous clinical outcomes help define appropriate populations, endpoints, and treatment conditions. A mitochondrial-support framework is proposed in which melatonin may preserve the cellular environment needed for GLP-1RA-mediated metabolic and survival responses. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide a promising foundation for developing combined GLP-1RA–melatonin strategies to preserve mitochondrial function, attenuate neuroinflammation, and support cognitive and functional recovery.

papers.title: Biological functions and emerging interplay of FGF21 and GDF15 in metabolic diseases and aging
papers.authors: Laura Salmón-Gómez; Susanne Keipert; Victoria Catalán; Amaia Rodríguez; Sara Becerril; Gema Frühbeck; Javier Gómez-Ambrosi
papers.abstract: Abstract Metabolic diseases and age-related disorders represent a major global health burden driven by the increasing prevalence of obesity and obesity-associated complications. These disorders are characterized by chronic disturbances in energy homeostasis. A key feature linking metabolic disease and aging is the activation of stress-related pathways, which contribute to progressive metabolic dysfunction. Among the endocrine mediators of cellular stress, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) have emerged as key regulators of metabolic homeostasis. Both are induced by similar stress conditions, including nutrient imbalance, inflammation, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and are elevated in pathophysiological conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and aging. FGF21 and GDF15 also share overlapping regulatory pathways and complementary functions, suggesting a potential coordinated regulation and functional interplay. However, the extent and physiological relevance of this possible interrelationship remain incompletely understood. This review summarizes current knowledge on the regulation, tissue sources, and signaling mechanisms of FGF21 and GDF15 across metabolic diseases and aging, with particular attention to their roles as mediators of adaptive metabolic responses and their overlapping biological actions. We further discuss their context-dependent effects under acute and chronic stress and their relevance as biomarkers of metabolic dysfunction and disease progression. Collectively, this work highlights FGF21 and GDF15 as integrated stress signals linking cellular stress to systemic metabolic adaptation, providing a conceptual framework for understanding their cooperative roles and regulation in metabolic and age-related diseases, which may have therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Ciliary-Mitochondrial Crosstalk in Cancer: Mechanistic Links Between Primary Cilium Dysfunction and Mitochondrial Reprogramming in Tumor Progression and Metastasis
papers.authors: Bonab MA, Tofighbakhsh Y, Shokri M, Behnam B.
papers.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
papers.abstract: Primary cilia are microtubule-based sensory organelles that coordinate key oncogenic signaling pathways, including Hedgehog, Wnt, PDGF, and TGF-β. Mitochondria, traditionally viewed as bioenergetic hubs, also regulate redox balance, calcium homeostasis, apoptosis, and metabolic plasticity. Emerging evidence demonstrates that these organelles are functionally coupled, forming a bidirectional ciliary-mitochondrial axis that influences cancer progression and metastasis. Disruption of ciliogenesis, often through IFT88 or KIF3A loss, impairs mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and promotes a glycolytic, biosynthetic phenotype. Conversely, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), and altered dynamics feedback to regulate ciliary assembly and signaling. Key mechanistic nodes include calcium flux, AMPK-ULK1 signaling, ROS-mediated communication, and the recently identified NDUFAF2-ARMC9 bridge linking mitochondrial metabolism to ciliogenesis. This crosstalk converges on pathways that drive epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, cancer stemness, migration, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. In the tumor microenvironment, hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, immune signaling, and extracellular vesicles further modulate this axis, contributing to metabolic heterogeneity and metastatic dissemination. Importantly, the relationship between cilia and cancer is context-dependent: cilia can be tumor-suppressive in some malignancies yet support oncogenic signaling in others. These insights suggest that targeting ciliary function, mitochondrial metabolism, or their intersection may offer novel therapeutic opportunities. This review synthesizes current evidence on ciliary-mitochondrial crosstalk, highlights unresolved mechanistic questions, and proposes an integrated framework for understanding how this organellar axis shapes cancer evolution and treatment response. We propose that integrated ciliary-mitochondrial signatures represent highly promising novel cancer biomarkers capable of predicting tumor plasticity, metastatic risk, and therapeutic response beyond conventional single-organelle or genomic markers.

papers.title: Differential redox-mitochondrial adaptation to ultra-high-dose-rate irradiation in astrocytes and glioma cells
papers.authors: Giulia Rosini; Elisa De Santis; Riccardo Nieri; Matteo Paolini; Filippo Rossi; Silverio Sbrana; Esther Ciarrocchi; Andrea Cavalieri; Fabiola Paiar; Fabio Di Martino; Eleonora Vannini; Mario Costa; Beatrice D’Orsi
papers.abstract: Abstract FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) delivers radiation at ultra-high dose rates (UHDRs) and has been reported to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying the ‘FLASH effect’ remain incompletely defined. FLASH-RT has been associated with differential normal and tumor tissue responses in preclinical studies, although the early cellular processes induced under these conditions remain incompletely understood. Here, we compared FLASH-RT versus conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in murine glioma GL261 cells and primary healthy astrocytic cultures, focusing on redox dynamics, mitochondrial function, bioenergetics, and transcriptional stress programs. Using real-time kinetic assays, flow cytometry, Seahorse analysis, and gene expression profiling, we found that in healthy astrocytes FLASH-RT reduced acute ROS accumulation, limited cell death, and was associated with greater preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential and respiratory capacity compared with CONV-RT. FLASH-RT was also associated with sustained induction of cell-cycle checkpoint and senescence-associated transcripts. In GL261 cells, FLASH-RT produced a lower initial ROS peak followed by continued ROS accumulation over time and enhanced G2/M accumulation, together with persistent mitochondrial depolarization and respiratory suppression. Annexin V analysis at 8 Gy revealed comparable levels of Annexin V positivity between FLASH- and CONV-RT, whereas FLASH-treated cells showed greater G2/M accumulation and metabolic dysfunction, consistent with altered cell-cycle progression rather than enhanced Annexin V-defined cell death. Pharmacological modulation with DPQ, Calpeptin, Nec-1 and zVAD differentially affected mitochondrial bioenergetic parameters across irradiation modalities and cell types, providing functional evidence for the potential contribution of distinct stress- and cell-death-associated signaling pathways to radiation-induced metabolic dysfunction. Similar stress responses were also observed in human U87 glioblastoma cells, where FLASH-RT induced stronger ROS accumulation, greater Annexin V positivity, and alterations in NAD⁺ levels associated with mitochondrial respiratory impairment compared with CONV-RT. Collectively, these data indicate that FLASH-RT elicits cell-type-specific redox–mitochondrial responses associated with relative preservation of mitochondrial function in healthy astrocytes and prolonged metabolic stress and altered cell-cycle dynamics in glioma cells, highlighting distinct early adaptations to FLASH irradiation in astrocytic and glioma models.

papers.title: Trehalose alleviates oxidative stress-induced senescence and is associated with cell-cycle remodeling.
papers.authors: Yu Yang; Honghan Chen; Ming Yang; Huan Li; Weitong Xu; Hui Gong; Yang Yang; Yuanliang Mo; Ning Huang; Jin Liu; Xiaoli Huang; Hengyi Xiao
papers.abstract: Trehalose has been widely used as a food and drug additive for a long time, and its effects on antioxidant stress, autophagy, and anti-aging have been gradually studied. However, the molecular mechanism by which trehalose exerts anti-oxidative stress and anti-aging effects has not been fully clarified. Our anti-aging cell phenotype study based on trehalose validates its intrinsic mechanisms of anti-oxidative stress and anti-inflammation in cells. We analyzed publicly available transcriptomic data (GSE76643) to identify molecular pathways regulated by trehalose, and then validated the key findings in our own cellular and animal experiments. The results indicate that trehalose alleviates oxidative stress-induced senescence, and that this effect is associated with remodeling of cell cycle progression, including down-regulation of selected cell-cycle regulators. The D-Gal-induced premature aging mouse model demonstrated that trehalose can effectively alleviate aging phenotypes in the hair, liver metabolic abnormalities, lung, and kidney of mice. Trehalose treatment reversed the D‑galactose‑induced upregulation of P16, P21, and P53 proteins in the liver, lung, and kidney, further supporting its anti‑aging effects in vivo. Additionally, the down-regulated expression of BIRC5, CCNE2, and CDK2 mRNA in certain tissues suggests that trehalose regulates or intervenes in the cell cycle. Based on the cell-cycle remodeling phenotype, we hypothesized that trehalose may modulate P65, STAT3, Keap1-Kelch, and CDK2. Molecular docking predicted potential interactions between trehalose and these proteins; these predictions require experimental validation. In conclusion, this study provides evidence that trehalose may alleviate oxidative stress-induced senescence in association with cell-cycle remodeling. These findings lay a foundation for further development of trehalose as an anti-aging intervention, but direct causality remains to be established.

papers.title: Universal protein immobilization and digestion reactor facilitates deep quantitative proteomic analysis of single Caenorhabditis elegans individuals
papers.authors: Wenjia Zhang; Yingyue Wang; Jiayu Tang; Lingxiao Weng; Guoquan Yan; Mingxia Gao; Xiangmin Zhang
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-organism proteomics can reveal heterogeneity masked by population-level measurements, but deep profiling of individual Caenorhabditis elegans remains challenging because of low protein input, inefficient extraction through the collagen-rich cuticle, and lengthy sample processing. Herein, we present SPIDR-C (single-organism protein immobilization and digestion reactor for C. elegans), a streamlined workflow enabling deep single-worm proteomics. SPIDR-C seamlessly integrates worm disruption, strong surfactant-assisted extraction, covalent protein immobilization, in-reactor sample cleanup, and rapid enzymatic digestion in a single-tube, transfer-free format. Built from commercially available insert tubes and requiring neither microfluidic devices nor custom instrumentation, the workflow is low-cost, easy to operate, and compatible with standard liquid chromatography (LC) autosamplers, allowing parallel batch processing of multiple samples within 2 h. By coupling aggressive extraction with LC−MS/MS-compatible cleanup, it enabled identification of more than 7100 proteins from a single adult worm, representing one of the deepest single-worm proteomes reported to date. Across eight single-worm-equivalent technical replicates, the median protein-abundance CV was 13.34%, with pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients above 0.977. We applied SPIDR-C to a high-glucose and high-fat (HGHF) model as an exploratory demonstration of its analytical utility, where single-worm proteomics captured HGHF-associated proteome alterations and individual-level heterogeneity under the same dietary challenge. Proteome profiling further pointed to two candidate HGHF-associated response patterns: one marked by higher abundance of ER proteostasis-related proteins and the other characterized by stronger lipid- and membrane-associated remodeling. Thus, SPIDR-C provides a practical strategy for deep single-organism proteomics and facilitates the investigation of molecular heterogeneity in complex low-input biological samples.

papers.title: 2,4-Dichlorophenol induced sex hormone imbalance in zebrafish ovary via esr1-mediated cholesterol synthesis inhibition.
papers.authors: Jiamin Shi; Rongjian Liu; Dongqiong Wei; Yang Zheng; Lei Yang; Samra; Cong Yuan; Yongmei Qi; Dejun Huang
papers.abstract: 2,4-Dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) is a persistent organic pollutant that disrupts endocrine homeostasis. Here, environmentally relevant concentrations of 2,4-DCP disrupted sex hormone balance in zebrafish, resulting in increased the ratios of estrogen (E2) to 11-ketotestosterone and E2 to testosterone, while inhibiting steroidogenesis pathway. However, the role of cholesterol as a precursor in this process remains unclear. Our results showed that 2,4-DCP significantly reduced the total cholesterol and free cholesterol in the ovary by downregulation of the genes srebp2 and hmgcr2 (for de novo synthesis of cholesterol), which decreased ovarian cholesterol availability. Consistently, inhibition of cholesterol synthesis using a specific inhibitor also significantly disrupted the sex hormone balance. Furthermore, 2,4-DCP exhibited anti-estrogenic effects in female zebrafish with high endogenous estrogen levels, as indicated by significantly suppressed the expression of esr1, esr2a and esr2b, as well as decreased vitellogenin levels. In the absence of estrogen, dual-luciferase reporter assays and point mutation studies confirmed that 2,4-DCP enhanced esr1/2b binding to the estrogen response element at the -452/-438 in the srebp2 promoter. These results indicated that 2,4-DCP inhibit cholesterol synthesis via competitive bindings to estrogen receptors. Then esr1 knockout zebrafish confirmed the key regulatory role of esr1 in cholesterol synthesis in vivo. Moreover, esr1 mRNA supplementation partially restored cholesterol synthesis and sex hormone level. These findings establish that 2,4-DCP impairs sex hormone balance by esr1-dependent transcriptional regulation of cholesterol synthesis, providing a theoretical basis for assessing the endocrine-disrupting effects of 2,4-DCP pollution in aquatic organisms.

papers.title: Ebola Virus VP40 C-terminal Lysine Residue Mediates Lipid Interactions and Dimer-Dimer Interactions.
papers.authors: Hannah M Woods; Yogesh B Narkhede; Ukesh Karki; Michael J Norris; Prem P Chapagain; Olaf Wiest; Robert V Stahelin
papers.abstract: The Ebola virus (EBOV) matrix protein VP40 is the main driver of viral assembly and budding, processes which depend on its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM). VP40 forms dimers in the cytoplasm that traffic to the membrane and assemble into higher-order oligomers, but the specific molecular determinants governing the stability of these oligomeric interfaces are not fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of the C-terminal lysine residue, Lys326, in mediating VP40-lipid and VP40-VP40 interactions. Using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and computational site-saturation mutagenesis, we predicted that while Lys326 has a minimal role in the stability of the isolated VP40 dimer, it is a critical determinant in stabilizing the interfaces of higher-order structures like tetramers and hexamers. Experimentally, mutation of this residue to alanine or aspartic acid (K326A or K326D) impaired VP40 PM localization, oligomerization, and in a charge-dependent manner, virus-like particle production. Our results indicate that a cationic residue is crucial not only for interactions with anionic phospholipids in the PM but, more importantly, for forming stabilizing networks across VP40 dimer-dimer interfaces. Together, these findings identify Lys326 as a keystone residue that couples membrane binding to the stabilization of essential higher-order oligomers, revealing a critical interface for EBOV assembly that could be exploited for future antiviral strategies.

papers.title: Effect of Atorvastatin and Rosuvastatin on Lipid Parameters and Inflammatory Biomarkers in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Aruba Sohail; Maman Khurshid; Aiman Khurshid; Muddassir Khalid; Areeba Raza; Mir Umer Farooq Alam Shah; Hira Khan
papers.abstract: Statins produce marked reductions in total and LDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein (CRP), and help prevent stroke, re-infarction, and subsequent risk of death. We conducted a meta-analysis to assess the role of atorvastatin in comparison with rosuvastatin in lowering levels of inflammatory biomarkers and lipid parameters in patients with ACS. Online databases were searched, and results from random-effects meta-analysis are presented as weighted mean differences (WMDs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. The outcomes were assessed at the short-term (≤1 month) and long-term (>3 months) follow-up. A total of 15 studies (13 RCTs and 2 observational studies) were included. The level of erythrocyte sedimentation rate ( P = 0.13), oxidized LDL ( P = 0.94), and long-term HDL-C ( P = 0.28) showed no significant difference between the two statin groups. No significant differences were observed between atorvastatin and rosuvastatin in total cholesterol and LDL-C at short-term or long-term follow-up. A significant decrease in CRP levels (WMD 4.08; 95% CI 1.53–6.63; P = 0.002; I 2 = 98%) and a significant rise in HDL-C (WMD −1.15; 95% CI −1.99 to −0.32; P = 0.007; I 2 = 39%) was reported in the rosuvastatin group compared to the atorvastatin group in the short-term. Atorvastatin was associated with a significant reduction in triglycerides at short-term follow-up (WMD −8.69; 95% CI −14.97 to −2.40; P = 0.007; I 2 = 35%), while the overall long-term comparison was borderline and did not reach conventional statistical significance. Our findings suggest that rosuvastatin may provide greater short-term reductions in CRP and modest increases in HDL-C compared with atorvastatin; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity and the absence of significant differences at longer follow-up.

papers.title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis and altered short-chain fatty acid biosynthetic pathways in Chinese children with obesity and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
papers.authors: Xin Yuan; Ying Zhang; Xiangquan Lin; Ruimin Chen
papers.abstract: Background Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), recently reclassified as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), is the most prevalent chronic liver disease in children, affecting 13% of the general pediatric population and up to 47% of children with obesity worldwide. Gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to NAFLD pathogenesis through the gut-liver axis, yet the interplay between microbial communities and host metabolic regulators, particularly angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4), remains incompletely characterized. Methods Eighty-nine Chinese children aged 5–15 years were enrolled, including 29 healthy controls (Con), 39 with simple obesity (OB), and 21 with obesity and NAFLD. Gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3–V4 region) and analyzed using QIIME2 and MicrobiomeAnalyst. Functional prediction employed PICRUSt2 referencing MetaCyc pathways. Serum ANGPTL4, leptin, adiponectin, and interleukin-6 were measured. Results Chao1 species richness differed significantly among groups (F = 4.98, p = 0.009), while Shannon diversity did not (F = 2.22, p = 0.115). Beta diversity (PERMANOVA, F = 2.87, R 2 = 0.063, p = 0.002) differed significantly among groups, although PERMDISP indicated heterogeneous dispersion (F = 6.62, p = 0.002). LEfSe analysis identified enrichment of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera (Bacteroides, Alistipes, Oscillospira, Parabacteroides) in healthy controls, while Megamonas, Blautia, Coprococcus, and Dorea characterized the NAFLD group. ANCOM-BC2 identified significant enrichment of Megamonas in the NAFLD group (q = 0.005 vs Con). PICRUSt2 predicted lower abundance of nine SCFA-related pathways in the obesity groups compared with controls. After FDR correction, Bacteroides-ANGPTL4 was the most significant correlation (r = 0.460, q < 0.001), and four additional associations survived correction. In hierarchical regression, Bacteroides remained independently associated with ANGPTL4 after adjustment for age, BMI, sex, and Tanner stage (β = 0.254, p = 0.016, ΔR 2 = 0.057), although this association was attenuated after additional adjustment for group status (β = 0.204, p = 0.058). Conclusion Chinese children with obesity and NAFLD exhibit gut microbial dysbiosis characterized by reduced species richness, depletion of SCFA-producing genera, and lower predicted abundance of SCFA-related pathways. The independent association between Bacteroides and ANGPTL4 suggests a potential microbiota-host metabolic link that may be associated with hepatic lipid metabolism.

papers.title: Hippocampal Glial Alterations Are Associated with Mitochondrial Changes and Reduced Glucocorticoid Receptor Density in Suicides
papers.authors: Andrea Judith Vázquez-Hernández; Yali Escribano-Cadena; Julio César Morales-Medina; Amira Flores; Laura Alejandra Mendoza-Larios; Roberto Cuauhtémoc Mendoza-Morales; Humberto Nicolini; Hiram Tendilla-Beltrán; Fernando García-Dolores; Gonzalo Flores
papers.abstract: Suicide is a major public health concern frequently associated with depressive disorders and neurobiological alterations within the hippocampus. This study investigated biomarkers related to neuroinflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and mitochondrial labeling in the CA1 region of the hippocampus of young and adult individuals of Mexican ancestry who died by suicide. Postmortem hippocampal CA1 samples were obtained from young and adult suicide cases and age-matched controls. Cellular markers of microglia (ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1, Iba1) and astrocytes (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP), neuronal density, glucocorticoid receptor expression, and mitochondrial labeling were evaluated and compared among groups. Suicide cases exhibited increased microglial and astrocyte cell density indicated by increased Iba1 and GFAP immunoreactivity in both age groups. In contrast, mitochondrial labeling and glucocorticoid receptor immunoreactivity were reduced in suicide cases, regardless of age. Additionally, a significant reduction in neuronal density was detected exclusively in young individuals who died by suicide. Together, these findings indicate age-independent alterations in glial immunoreactivity, mitochondrial labeling, and glucocorticoid receptor expression, alongside reduced neuronal density in the hippocampal CA1 region of younger suicide cases, supporting the involvement of neuroinflammation-related processes in suicide. Despite the limited sample size, these findings provide insight into potential neurobiological mechanisms underlying suicide and may contribute to the identification of biomarkers and therapeutic targets for individuals at risk.

papers.title: Immunotherapy targeting an endogenous retrovirus decreases islet senescence markers and preserves glucose control in a mouse model of type 2 diabetes.
papers.authors: Daniel Bjørklund Andersen; Nanna Skeltved; Gabriel Mira González; Thomas Garde-Due; Iker Ausina; Clara Iacumin; Lasse Neukirch; Anne-Marie Andersson; Emeline Ragonnaud; Joachim Størling; Claus Desler; Frederik Otzen Bagger; Kaare Villum Grunddal; Peter Johannes Holst
papers.abstract: Type-2-diabetes is characterized by progressive metabolic stress and accumulation of senescent cells in key metabolic tissues, such as the pancreas, adipose tissue, and liver. Cellular senescence - an irreversible growth-arrested, and pro-inflammatory cell state can lead to induction of endogenous retrovirus (ERV) expression, which can also trigger cellular senescence. This possibly implies that a self-reinforcing ERV-senescence axis contributes to the metabolic decline and T2D. Here we developed and tested a mouse endogenous retrovirus (muERV) based active immunotherapy targeted at the most intact muERV, IAPE (Intracisternal A-type Particles elements with an Envelope) to eliminate cells expressing muERVs and senescence associated proteins in a mouse model of accelerated diabetes combining a high-fat diet (HFD) with dexamethasone (DEX) and streptozotocin (STZ) (DS-HFD). Immunized DS-HFD mice (DS-HFD + IAPE-Tx) showed increased B and T cell responses towards IAPE. Antisera generated using our IAPE-targeted active immunotherapy was used to confirm activation of IAPE expression in the murine β-cell line MIN-6, following both inflammatory (cytokines) and chemical stress (STZ and DEX). In Vivo, DS-HFD + IAPE-Tx mice showed reduced weight gain, improved fasting insulin-glucose homeostasis and oral glucose tolerance. They furthermore showed reduction in histomorphometry features consistent with steatosis, hepatocyte binucleation, reduced adipocyte size, and pancreatic islet senescence markers p16INK4a and p21Cip1/waf1, with a slight decrease in islet IAPE. Finally, we show activation of a human orthologue to IAPE, HERV-K, in cytokine-exposed isolated human pancreatic islets and EndoC-βH5 β-cells. Together, our results suggest that ERV antigens are expressed in metabolic disease models and may be targeted by immunotherapy to improve metabolic parameters, through a potential senolytic or senostatic-related but so far undefined mechanism.

papers.title: In Silico Evidence for Enterobactin-Facilitated Ferric Iron Import into Mitochondria via ATP Synthase Alpha Subunit Binding
papers.authors: Abeg Dutta; Anutthaman Parthasarathy; Ganesh Pandian Namasivayam
papers.abstract: Research on mitochondrial iron metabolism has largely focused on Fe(II), as it is relatively soluble and readily available under physiological conditions. By contrast, the role of Fe(III) remains less well understood. Its poor solubility and tendency to form potentially harmful ferric hydroxides mean that it must remain bound to suitable ligands or chaperones during transport. Canonically, iron is delivered to cells via transferrin (Tf), which binds the transferrin receptor (TfR1) for receptor-mediated endocytosis. Acidification of endosomes releases Fe(III), which is then reduced to Fe(II) by STEAP3 and transported into the cytosol by DMT1, forming a labile iron pool for mitochondrial use. However, the direct trafficking of Fe(III) into mitochondria has remained unexplored. Here, we propose a potential model for Fe(III) uptake into mitochondria through enterobactin, a bacterial siderophore known to influence host iron metabolism. Using in silico docking with AutoDock Vina and AlphaFold2-derived mitochondrial F-type ATP synthase structures, we observe that Fe(III)- enterobactin complexes yield docking scores comparable to Fe(II)-enterobactin complexes at the ATP synthase alpha subunit. In addition, enterobactin itself adopts compatible binding poses at the protein surface. These observations are consistent with a possible interaction framework but do not establish a dissociative mechanism for iron delivery within the mitochondrial matrix. These docking analyses support the structural plausibility of an enterobactin-associated ferric iron interaction with the mitochondrial ATP synthase alpha subunit. Although these findings do not establish a specific transport mechanism, they raise the possibility of an alternative route for mitochondrial iron trafficking. Further experimental work is needed to determine whether this pathway operates in cells and how it contributes to iron homeostasis. More broadly, the proposed model suggests a possible connection between microbial siderophores and mitochondrial iron handling, with potential physiological and pathological relevance.

papers.title: Mitochondrial genome editing reveals the impact of complex I heteroplasmic variants on human neurogenesis
papers.authors: Tolle, I.; Fiorini, C.; Dobner, J.; Zink, A.; Pasti, A. P.; Balmaceda, V.; Tschuschke, F.; Herebian, D.; Mayatepek, E.; Bottani, E.; Lisowski, P.; Carelli, V.; Rossi, A.; Prigione, A.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants, whether maternally inherited or acquired somatically during aging, can be particularly detrimental to cells that rely on mitochondrial metabolism such as neurons. The functional consequences of mtDNA variants are thought to depend on their heteroplasmy, defined as the proportion of mtDNA molecules carrying that variant. However, investigating the specific effects of heteroplasmic mtDNA variants on human neuronal function has been challenging. Studies using patient-derived cells cannot conclusively attribute observed phenotypes to a single mtDNA variant, while conventional genome editing approaches are not applicable to mtDNA. Here, we use DddA-derived cytosine base editor (DdCBE) to introduce pathogenic heteroplasmic mtDNA variants into Neurogenin 2 (NGN2)-inducible human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We focus on two variants in the genes MT-ND1 and MT-ND5 belonging to complex I (CI), the largest component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and a frequent contributor to human disease, including the incurable neurodevelopmental disorder Leigh syndrome. mtDNA-edited iPSC lines exhibit low off-target editing and maintain similar heteroplasmy following subclonal isolation and differentiation into NGN2-induced neurons (iNs). Although the CI variants do not substantially affect mitochondrial energy metabolism in undifferentiated iPSCs, they reduce mitochondrial membrane potential in iNs where they drive a transcriptional reprogramming indicative of impaired neuronal commitment. These findings suggest that heteroplasmic CI variants are sufficient to disrupt neural fate specification even at relatively low heteroplasmy. More broadly, mtDNA editing in human iPSCs provides a powerful platform to investigate how mitochondrial fitness and heteroplasmy influence development and disease.

papers.title: Role of the ACTH-SF1/NR5A1-NRF2 axis in glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical cell death through mitochondrial ROS accumulation
papers.authors: Naohiro Uchida; Namiko Kawamura; Hironobu Umakoshi; Maki Yokomoto-Umakoshi; Tazuru Fukumoto; Norifusa Iwahashi; Masamichi Fujita; Aya Fujimoto; Kaede Saito; Yuta Hiraike; Fumiya Takahashi; Takashi Baba; Masahide Seki; Yutaka Suzuki; Yoshihiro Ogawa
papers.abstract: Abstract Exogenous glucocorticoids are widely used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, yet the prolonged administration often leads to adrenocortical atrophy and subsequent adrenal insufficiency. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical atrophy remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that adrenocortical alterations in dexamethasone (DEX)-treated mice are similar to those in human adrenocortical tissues adjacent to cortisol-producing adenoma. During DEX treatment, marked cell death occurs, being restricted to the adrenocortical zona fasciculata (ZF), as a result of reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction; the pathological changes are all attenuated by co-administration of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In DEX-treated mice, ACTH deficiency impairs nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-dependent redox homeostasis in ZF cells. Activation of the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway, a downstream signaling of ACTH stimulation, increases gene expression of steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1; NR5A1) in cultured adrenocortical cells in vitro, where it binds directly to the Nrf2 promoter and enhances its transcription, thereby promoting antioxidant gene expression to maintain redox homeostasis. This study highlights the role of the ACTH-SF1-NRF2 axis in glucocorticoid-induced adrenocortical cell death through mitochondrial ROS accumulation, thereby providing a clue to a new therapeutic strategy to prevent or treat secondary adrenal insufficiency during glucocorticoid excess.

papers.title: Structural Determinants Underlying the Interplay Between Fatty Acid Binding and S-Nitrosylation of Human Serum Albumin
papers.authors: Anastasia A. Batalova; Kamila V. Samodurova; Mikhail A. Vovk; Daria A. Belinskaia; Richard O. Jenkins; Nikolay V. Goncharov
papers.abstract: Human serum albumin (HSA) is a multifunctional protein whose biological properties are determined not only by its amino acid sequence but also by a complex interplay of functional sites, post-translational modifications, and endogenous ligands. However, the structural mechanisms by which these regulatory factors influence the functional state of HSA remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the structural basis of the interplay between HSA functional regions, using Cys34 S-nitrosylation and fatty acid (FA) binding as model regulatory processes. For this purpose, the structural features and conformational dynamics of FA-free and FA-loaded native and nitrosylated HSA, as well as their interactions with glutathione (GSH) and S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), were studied using molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Changes in the overall structure of HSA after incubation with GSNO were assessed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. MD analysis revealed that FA binding alters the conformational dynamics of HSA and affects the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. These FA-induced effects were further modulated by S-nitrosylation, which influenced the conformational landscape of albumin in a manner dependent on its fatty acid-bound state. The similarity of the one-dimensional 1H NMR spectra of HSA before and after incubation with GSNO suggests the absence of pronounced changes in the overall protein structure upon interaction with the nitrosylating agent. The obtained data provide insights into how FA binding and S-nitrosylation shape the conformational properties of HSA through modulation of the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. The results highlight the importance of considering post-translational modifications and endogenous ligands as key determinants of HSA structure–function relationships.

Results The 60 mg/kg TSA group exhibited improved memory in Y-maze tests, with elevated spontaneous alternation rate ( p p p p p p Conclusions This study reveals TSA's preventive potential against Alzheimer's disease by modulating inflammation-associated lipid metabolism in APP/PS1 mice.

It survives adjustment for conservation, burial and coverage, and is concentrated in ND1 within 15 of the quinone cavity, not spread along the proton path. papers.title: Clinical and genetic spectrum in a cohort of patients with suspected mitochondrial disease
papers.authors: Doina Secu; Daniela Blanita; Natalia Usurelu; Calin Deleanu; Alina Nicolescu; Victoria Sacara
papers.abstract: Introduction : Mitochondrial diseases (MDs) are a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders affecting oxidative phosphorylation, characterized by diverse neuromuscular and multisystemic manifestations, whose clinical variability and genetic complexity necessitate a comprehensive, multidisciplinary diagnostic approach. Aim : This study aims to explore the phenotypic and genotypic spectrum of patients with suspected MD, focusing on mitochondrial genome variations to improve diagnostic accuracy and support genetic counseling. Materials and methods : We analyzed 240 patients with a Nijmegen mitochondrial disease score (NMDS) ≥3, with 90 individuals undergoing comprehensive clinical, biochemical, neuroimaging, and genetic assessments. Descriptive statistics were applied to summarize clinical and biochemical data, while inferential analyses, including chi-square tests and regression models, were employed to explore genotype-phenotype associations. Results : The study delineated a multifaceted clinical spectrum, with neuromuscular dysfunction as the predominant hallmark, evidenced by a high prevalence of developmental delay (88.9%), hypotonia (77.8%), and exercise intolerance (63.3%). Patients with mitochondrial involvement displayed a significantly greater burden of neurological (seizures: 71.9% vs. 43.1%, p =0.009) and cardiac abnormalities (37.5% vs. 15.5%, p =0.018), underscoring their diagnostic relevance. Genetic analysis identified gene variants associated with the patients’ phenotypes in 35.6% of cases, with Complex I being the most frequently affected, emphasizing its pivotal role in mitochondrial dysfunction and disease severity. Conclusion : Our findings highlight the genetic and clinical heterogeneity of MDs, emphasizing the importance of integrating molecular, biochemical, and neuroimaging data to enhance early diagnosis and facilitate personalized treatment strategies.

papers.title: Comparison of 3 guideline lipid emulsion regimens for local anesthetic systemic toxicity: an in silico study of bolus duration, total dose, and treatment delay in intravenous bupivacaine overdose.
papers.authors: Sunho Lim; Sooyoung Cho; Eunbi Cho
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Lipid emulsion is the only specific antidote for local anesthetic systemic toxicity, but no dose-finding study has been conducted. We compared 3 published regimens and alternative schedules that deliver the same dose in different ways using a human model of intravenous bupivacaine overdose. METHODS: A 14-compartment human bupivacaine model was independently reimplemented without fitted parameters, replacing first-order lipid elimination with a saturable term. Toxicity was modeled as 112.5 mg administered intravenously over 3 minutes. Benefit was defined as the predicted maximum decrease in myocardial bupivacaine within 30 minutes, and harm as the predicted relative lipid load, indexed by peak plasma triglyceride concentration. Neither measure is a validated surrogate. RESULTS: The 3 guidelines specify the same doses but different bolus durations: 1 minute versus 2-3 minutes. At a matched dose of 12 mL/kg, myocardial bupivacaine decreased by 30.5% with the 1-minute bolus and 24.9% with the 2.5-minute bolus, with the same lipid load. The completed American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine regimen (7.64 mL/kg) achieved a 24.6% decrease versus 24.9% with 12 mL/kg; thus, complete regimens differ in schedule as well as dose. Repeating the 1-minute bolus twice, for a total of 4.5 mL/kg, achieved a 31.9% decrease with 62% less emulsion. Start time had the greatest effect: the best regimen achieved a 41.8% decrease when started at the end of the injection, but only 9.6% when started at 10 minutes. CONCLUSION: In this bupivacaine model, bolus duration distinguished the regimens more than dose did, and delay had a greater effect than either, eliminating most of the benefit without changing the lipid load. Treatment should begin at the first signs of toxicity, and 20% lipid emulsion should be immediately available wherever local anesthetics are used.

papers.title: Dietary Lipid Sources and Lysolecithin Modulate Growth, Lipid Metabolism, Hepatopancreatic Health, and Intestinal Microbiota in Macrobrachium rosenbergii.
papers.authors: Zongsheng Qiu; Xinyi Wei; Jianle Yang; Yuqiang Wei; Shasha Liu; Jianhua Zhao; Qiyou Xu; Clement R de Cruz
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of dietary lipid sources and lysolecithin (LL) supplementation on the growth performance, lipid metabolism, hepatopancreatic histology, and intestinal microbiota of Macrobrachium rosenbergii. A 56-day feeding trial was conducted using six isonitrogenous diets containing fish oil (FO), soybean oil (SO), or a 1:1 FO-SO blend (mixed oil [MO]), and each supplemented with or without 0.5% LL. Results indicated a significant interaction between dietary lipid sources and LL supplementation on growth performance (p < 0.05). The MO diet supplemented with LL yielded the highest growth rates, while LL supplementation significantly improved feed efficiency (p < 0.05). Regarding histological status, the dietary SO treatment induced a significant increase in hepatopancreatic lipid deposition (p < 0.0001) and histological alterations, while LL supplementation reduced lipid deposition and improved hepatopancreatic morphology. Dietary lipid source significantly affected muscle n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs; p < 0.01). However, a significant interaction between dietary lipid source and LL supplementation was observed specifically for hepatopancreatic total n-3 PUFA (p = 0.0053). Gene expression analysis confirmed that LL modulates lipid metabolism in a source-dependent manner, upregulating fatty acid oxidation pathways (Pparα and Cpt1) in FO groups while influencing synthesis pathways (FAS) in SO groups (p < 0.05). Furthermore, LL supplementation significantly altered the composition of intestinal microbiota, specifically enriching beneficial bacterial genera in dietary SO-treatment (p < 0.05). In conclusion, the dietary treatment combining MOs and LL showed beneficial effects on growth performance, lipid metabolism, and hepatopancreatic health in M. rosenbergii.

papers.title: Differential reproductive effects of two insect growth regulators (20-hydroxyecdysone and methyl farnesoate) on non-target aquatic organism: A case study using Daphnia magna.
papers.authors: Meng You; Yu Yang; Xinyu Chang; Yuting Zhang; Tao Wang; Hongyan Zhang; Runbing Xu
papers.venue: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Toxicology & pharmacology : CBP
papers.abstract: Two insect growth regulators (IGRs), 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) and methyl farnesoate (MF), are widely used in hormone-based pest control and may pose risks to aquatic ecosystems by disrupting the endocrine systems of non-target organisms. This study investigated the chronic (21-day) and acute (96-h) toxic effects of hazard characterization dose (50 μg/L) 20E and MF on reproduction, endocrine disruption, and underlying molecular mechanisms in Daphnia magna, a key model in ecotoxicology. Chronic exposure revealed that 20E significantly enhanced somatic growth (+5.4% body length at day 7) while inhibiting reproduction (-14.95% total offspring), whereas MF had no significant effects in surviving individuals, but suppressed overall reproduction through a mortality-driven effect. Acute exposure demonstrated that 20E elevated vitellogenin (+45.33%) and ecdysone levels (+22.09%), while MF primarily increased juvenile hormone (JH) synthesis (+7.99%). Transcriptomic analysis revealed that both compounds downregulated sphingolipid and glycerophospholipid metabolism pathways, with shared downregulation of MFE (Methyl farnesoate epoxidase) and EPPL (Ethanolamine-phosphate phospho-lyase) genes critical for JH and lipid homeostasis. Molecular docking predicted that 20E and MF could bind to the ecdysone receptor (EcR) and methoprene-tolerant (Met) proteins, with MF showing higher binding affinity to EcR (-6.95 kcal/mol vs. -6.05 kcal/mol for 20E). These endocrine disruptions are consistent with the suppression of reproduction via altered cholesterol mobilization and steroidogenesis pathways. This study provides novel insights into the mechanisms of estrogenic disruption in D. magna, highlighting the ecological risks of IGRs in aquatic environments.

papers.title: Electrochemical Features and Mechanism of Steel Corrosion Inhibition by Inhibitors Derived from Beef Tallow Fatty Acids
papers.authors: Oleksandr Romanchuk; Petro Topilnytskyy; Viktoria Romanchuk
papers.abstract: Ensuring the long-term operation of structural materials in heterophase oil and gas environments requires the development of effective, environmentally safe methods of anti-corrosion protection. The work aims to study the anti-corrosion efficiency and electrochemical behavior of new modified inhibitors based on higher distilled fatty acids derived from beef fat (MSEA, DSEA, DHEA) under conditions of iron acid corrosion. The objectives of the study included determining the kinetic parameters of the corrosion process and establishing the mechanism of the synthesized compounds' action at a concentration of 50 ppm using the potentiodynamic polarization method. Electrochemical measurements were performed in triplicate in a model corrosive environment of 0.1M HCl + butan-1-ol with subsequent calculation of standard deviations for the obtained values. The results of polarization studies showed a significant decrease in the corrosion current density for all modifications. The highest protective ability was observed for the DHEA compound. The positive direction of the potential shift and the nature of the change in the Tafel slopes indicate that within the general mixed mechanism of adsorption of compounds, there is a predominant kinetic inhibition of the anodic dissolution of the metal. The results obtained are consistent with previous gravimetric data and confirm the promising application of the synthesized alkanolamides for the protection of equipment in acidic environments.

papers.title: Identification of ageing-related genes in prostate cancer with type 2 Diabetes using machine learning: a multi-omics study focusing on SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4.
papers.authors: Zhang W, Zhang X, Zhang C, Shi X, Deng Y, Gao Y, Bi K, Wang Z, Chen G, Ye Z, An Z, Fu W.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) demonstrates complex associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and ageing, though their interconnected molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify and validate diagnostic biomarkers at the intersection of these pathways to enable early detection and risk stratification in high-risk populations. Bioinformatic analysis was performed on PCa and T2DM transcriptomic data downloaded from the GEO database, followed by differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment. Eight machine learning algorithms were applied to identify hub ageing-related genes (ARGs), with SHAP analysis interpreting feature importance. A nomogram model was constructed and validated across multiple cohorts. Immune infiltration, drug sensitivity, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics were used for mechanistic exploration. Three key ARGs (SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4) were identified and used to develop a diagnostic model with high accuracy (AUCs: 0.726-0.905). SOX4 promoted immune evasion, PRNP exhibited context-dependent duality, and FOXO4 functioned as a tumor suppressor. Spatial and single-cell analyses revealed cell-type-specific expression and fibroblast-epithelial communication via MIF, LRP1, and FZD1. Drug sensitivity profiling identified abiraterone and docetaxel as potential therapeutics for high- and low-risk patients, respectively. In conclusion, SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4 are key biomarkers linking PCa, T2DM, and ageing, and the diagnostic model shows robust performance and clinical utility, providing insights into microenvironment-driven mechanisms and personalized treatment strategies for PCa patients with T2DM.

papers.title: Lipid-based nanoencapsulation prolongs the antinociceptive effect of cannabidiol in experimental neuropathic pain.
papers.authors: Thalita da Cruz Monteiro Santana; Anna Beatriz de Oliveira Cruz; Lucas Gabriel da Silva Oliveira; Pedro Santana Sales Lauria; Daniele Brustolim; Eryvaldo Sócrates Tabosa do Egito; Max Denisson Maurício Viana; Cristiane Flora Villarreal
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP) is a debilitating chronic condition frequently refractory to available therapies, while the therapeutic potential of cannabidiol (CBD) is limited by its unfavorable physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties. This study investigated whether incorporation of CBD into a lipid-based microemulsion (LS-CBD) could improve its antinociceptive profile in a murine model of NP, and explored potential molecular mechanisms and safety. LS-CBD was prepared by a high-energy emulsification method and exhibited nanometric droplet size, narrow size distribution, high entrapment efficiency (96.8 ± 0.7%), and physicochemical stability over 60 days. Male C57BL/6 mice subjected to partial sciatic nerve ligation were evaluated for mechanical and thermal nociception following acute and repeated oral administration of CBD and LS-CBD (25, 50, and 75 mg/kg). Compared with free CBD, LS-CBD prolonged the duration of thermal antinociception (1-8 h vs. 2 h) and produced a significantly greater global antinociceptive effect. Peak antinociception did not differ between formulations (50.0 ± 14.9% vs. 53.2 ± 25.5%), indicating that nanoencapsulation prolonged the response rather than increasing its magnitude. Under repeated administration, LS-CBD produced significant mechanical antinociceptive activity on every day of the seven-day treatment period, while both formulations produced comparable and sustained thermal antinociception without evidence of tolerance development. At the molecular level, both CBD and LS-CBD increased Sod1 and Cat transcripts relative to naive animals, and reduced Nos2 and Gfap transcripts relative to neuropathic controls, in the dorsal root ganglia, suggesting attenuation of nitrosative stress and satellite glial cell activation. Neither treatment induced hematological, biochemical, or body weight alterations following repeated administration. These findings support lipid-based nanoencapsulation as a strategy to extend the duration of CBD antinociception after oral administration.

papers.title: Neuronal receptor remodeling in the aging periosteum: From single-cell atlases to regenerative targets
papers.authors: Ziyu Liu; Jianguo Qi; Yong Liu; Hongshang Chu
papers.abstract: Abstract The periosteum is the most densely innervated compartment of the skeleton and harbors periosteal stem cells expressing a broad repertoire of neuronal receptors traditionally associated with the nervous system. This narrative review aimed to map the neuronal receptor landscape of the periosteum and its age-dependent remodeling, and to evaluate the therapeutic implications of these receptors for age-related skeletal disorders. Literature was identified using a structured, PRISMA-informed search strategy across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from database inception. Eligible studies addressed neuronal receptor expression or signaling in periosteal tissue, periosteal stem and progenitor cells, or bone. Additionally, an exploratory reanalysis of the publicly available GSE297256 single-cell transcriptomic dataset was performed to contextualize the literature synthesis; no unpublished data were included. The literature synthesis delineated seven major neuronal receptor families in periosteal homeostasis: semaphorin-neuropilin, neurotrophin-Trk, Slit-Robo, adrenergic, cannabinoid, purinergic, and sensory neuropeptide systems. Restricting the analysis to bona fide neuronal receptors, 29 receptor genes were actively transcribed in periosteal stem cells, with neuropilin 2 ( Nrp2 ) ranking highest by a composite score integrating expression magnitude, detection frequency, and cell-type specificity. In exploratory cell-level analysis, Nrp2 expression showed a progressive age-associated increase from young (log1p mean 1.35) to middle-aged (1.85) to old (2.70) mice, concomitant with a decline of Postn-expressing Osteo-X progenitors and activation of stress-response genes ( Mt1 , Mt2 , Gadd45b , and Cebpd ), and was associated with dysregulation of the axon guidance ligand Slit2, downregulation of osteocalcin-associated genes ( Bglap and Bglap2 ), and predicted upstream regulation by the vitamin D receptor, implicating a vitamin D receptor- Nrp2 axis in periosteal aging. Age-related periosteal dysfunction, including cambium layer thinning, progenitor decline, and impaired progenitor-immune crosstalk, paralleled this receptor dysregulation. Neuronal receptor modulation, including Bdnf -TrkB, Sema3a-Nrp1 , and Nrp2 -targeted strategies, emerges as a promising multimodal approach for skeletal regeneration and aging intervention, warranting functional and clinical validation.

papers.title: Standard treatment against paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma promotes senescence and sensitizes tumours to BCL-xL inhibition
papers.authors: Romain Guiho; Hiba Hamdi; Grace Cooksley; Timoty H Chang; Lei Cao; Romain Sigaud; Sophie Bliss; Ashley Vardon; Scott Haston; Florian Selt; Akang Leonard Bassey; Daniela Kocher; Ria Kedia; Daniel Gharai; Jesús Gil; Olaf Witt; Till Milde; Darren Hargrave; Paula Alexandre; Pratiti Bandopadhayay; Juan Pedro Martinez Barbera
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Chemo-, radio-, and targeted therapies can induce a stable growth arrest known as therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which may be therapeutically exploited using senolytic compounds that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Children with BRAF-V600E-driven brain tumours are commonly treated with low-dose chemotherapies and MAPK inhibitors, alone or in combination, often with good initial responses. However, a majority of patients experiences tumour regrowth following treatment withdrawal. Here, we investigate the contribution of TIS to treatment response and relapse, and assess the therapeutic potential of senolytics in preclinical models of paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma. Methods Preclinical models of paediatric low-grade glioma were analysed in vitro or following orthotopic transplantation into mice and treated with Dabrafenib, Trametinib, Tovorafenib or Vinblastine. Senescence was assessed using molecular and cytological markers. Sensitivity to senolytic compounds was evaluated using in vitro dose-response assays and in vivo treatment studies. Results Trametinib induced a robust senescent phenotype in BT-40 tumours in vivo, characterised by activation of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype and expansion of IBA-1-positive myeloid cells. In vitro, senescence was induced in BT-40 cells following treatment with MAPK inhibitors and Vinblastine, and was similarly observed in H9-derived human neural stem cells expressing BRAF-V600E. Navitoclax was identified as a potent senolytic against senescent BT-40 cells, primarily through inhibition of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-xL. In vivo, combined Trametinib and Navitoclax treatment ablated senescent tumour cells, significantly reduced tumour regrowth after treatment withdrawal, and improved survival. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that Navitoclax enhances Trametinib's anti-tumour efficacy and limits tumour relapse following treatment cessation.

papers.title: TMEM63B as a dual-function mechanosensitive channel and lipid scramblase: structural insights, physiological roles, and pharmacological potential.
papers.authors: Zihan Chang; Zhirong Wang; Jiayi Tong; Yakun Yu; Jieyu Qi; Renjie Chai; Yanfeng Wang
papers.abstract: TMEM63B, a member of the transmembrane channel/scramblase (TCS) superfamily, functions as both a mechanosensitive and osmosensitive ion channel and a lipid scramblase. Recent structural and functional studies have begun to reveal the molecular basis underlying these dual functions. In this review, we summarize the current understanding of TMEM63B, focusing on its structural architecture, channel and scramblase conformations, activation mechanisms, physiological roles and therapeutic potential. Importantly, the broad tissue distribution and disease-associated mutations of TMEM63B-linked to developmental epileptic encephalopathy, hemolytic anemia, placental dysfunction, pulmonary insufficiency, and intestinal barrier defects-underscore its emerging pharmacological relevance. We discuss the therapeutic opportunities and challenges in targeting TMEM63B, including allosteric modulation of its mechanosensitive gating, isoform- and tissue-selective strategies to mitigate on-target off-tissue toxicity, and the potential of biologics such as the agonistic antibody YN9303-24 for loss-of-function disorders. These insights provide a framework for understanding the mechanistic diversity of TCS proteins, their physiological significance, and their translational potential as a new class of druggable mechanosensitive targets.
